---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/config/config-file-names.md
---
# Config file names

A `dbx.config.*` file is **optional**: the recommended setup carries the config
inline in the `dbx()` Vite plugin inside `vite.config.*`. When a project uses a
config file, the loader looks for, in order:

```
dbx.config.ts
dbx.config.mts
dbx.config.js
dbx.config.mjs
dbx.config.cjs
dbx.config.json
```

A TS/JS config is imported through `tsx` with the nearest `tsconfig.json`, so
it can use the project's path aliases and `.js` specifiers that point at `.ts`
sources. See [Loader](/guide/config/loader) for the `toolchain.loader` section,
custom tsconfigs and examples.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/config/defineconfig.md
---
# `defineConfig`

`defineConfig` is an identity helper that gives the file full type-checking and
autocomplete (it mirrors Vite's `defineConfig`). Like Vite, the argument may be a
plain object, a promise, or a sync/async callback — the loader resolves it, so a
config can do async work before returning `{ toolchain }`:

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig(async () => {
    const { readFile } = await import('node:fs/promises');
    const version = (await readFile('./VERSION', 'utf-8')).trim();

    return {
        toolchain: {
            project: { name: 'myapp', nodeVersion: version },
        },
    };
});
```

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/config/hooks.md
---
# Hooks

`.ts`/`.js` configs can declare lifecycle hooks (JSON cannot):

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        hooks: {
            afterLoad: ({ tokens }) => console.log(tokens),
            beforeSync: ctx => ctx.log('syncing...'),
            afterTask: ({ task, files }) => console.log(task.name, files?.length),
            afterSync: ({ result }) => console.log(result.written.length),
            beforeVersion: ({ previousVersion, version }) =>
                console.log(`${previousVersion} -> ${version}`),
            afterVersion: ({ version }) => console.log('released', version),
            onChange: ({ path }) => console.log('changed', path),
        },
    },
});
```

Return values are awaited.

## `beforeVersion`

`beforeVersion` runs after the bump is planned and **before** `dbx changelog`
writes the new versions or changelogs. It receives the repository root, the
planned `version` and the `previousVersion`:

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
hooks: {
    beforeVersion: async ({ cwd, previousVersion, version }) => {
        await assertReleaseAllowed(previousVersion, version, cwd);
    },
},
```

Throwing (or a rejected async hook) aborts the run before any files are
written. It does not run for `--dry-run`, `--release-body` or `--format-only`.

## `afterVersion`

`afterVersion` runs after `dbx changelog` writes the new versions and
changelogs (it does not run for `--dry-run`, `--release-body` or
`--format-only`). It receives the repository root and the new version:

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
hooks: {
    afterVersion: async ({ cwd, version }) => {
        console.log('released', version);
        await updateScaffoldCatalog(cwd);
    },
},
```

Async hooks are awaited by the CLI and `runChangelogAsync`; the synchronous
`runChangelog` wrapper rejects async hooks. A failing `beforeVersion` hook aborts
the run before any files are written (a failing `afterVersion` hook runs after
the writes). The changelog workflow stages `.yarnrc.yml` together with
`package.json`/`CHANGELOG.md`, so hooks that update a scaffold catalog are
committed in the same version-bump commit.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/config/loader.md
---
# Loader

The `toolchain.loader` section controls how `dbx.config.*` files are imported.
A TS/JS config is loaded through [`tsx`](https://tsx.is), so it can use the
project's TypeScript path aliases and import `.ts` sources with a `.js`
specifier.

## Options

| Option     | Type                | Default | Description                                                             |
| ---------- | ------------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `tsconfig` | `boolean \| string` | `true`  | The tsconfig used to resolve imports. `true` = nearest `tsconfig.json`. |

* `true` (default) — use the nearest `tsconfig.json` above the config file
  (the workspace's own).
* `"path/to/tsconfig.json"` — use a different tsconfig. The path is resolved
  from the project root.
* `false` — disable tsconfig resolution. Relative `.js` → `.ts` rewriting still
  works, but tsconfig `paths` aliases do not.

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
import { defineConfig } from '@deltabox/toolchain';

export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        loader: { tsconfig: 'tsconfig.loader.json' },
    },
});
```

`loader` is repository-scoped: it is **not merged into a nested workspace's
config**. A nested config uses its parent's loader choice when it does not set
one itself.

## Path aliases and source extensions

With the default loader, imports resolve the way the project's TypeScript does:

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
import { shared } from '@org/shared/config.js'; // shared/config.ts

import { defineConfig } from '@deltabox/toolchain';

export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        project: shared.project,
    },
});
```

The loader rewrites these specifiers when the target exists:

| Import         | Resolves to                    |
| -------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `./helper.js`  | `helper.ts`, `helper.tsx`, ... |
| `./helper.mjs` | `helper.mts`                   |
| `./helper.cjs` | `helper.cts`                   |
| `./helper.jsx` | `helper.tsx`                   |

It also follows a tsconfig's relative `extends` chain for `baseUrl` / `paths`.
A genuinely missing package or module is still an error: the loader does not
silently turn it into an empty module.

## Programmatic API

`loadToolchainConfig` accepts the same override directly:

```ts
import { loadToolchainConfig } from '@deltabox/toolchain';

const loaded = await loadToolchainConfig(process.cwd(), {
    loaderTsconfig: 'tsconfig.loader.json', // or false
});
```

The option takes precedence over the config's own `loader.tsconfig` and over
the parent config's choice. When omitted, the loader uses the config's
`loader.tsconfig`, then the parent config's, then the nearest `tsconfig.json`.

## Notes

* The loader reads `loader.tsconfig` from the config it is loading, so the
  first import must already be resolvable. Put a shared choice on the root
  config (it is used for nested configs) or point the nearest `tsconfig.json`
  at it.
* `.json` configs are parsed directly and do not use a tsconfig.

## Reusing the loader in another project

`@deltabox/toolchain/config` exposes the same building blocks for consumers with
their own config format:

```ts
import {
    collect,
    createConfigFile,
    loadConfig,
    loadConfigSync,
    parseCliConfig,
    parseConfig,
    parseEnvConfig,
} from '@deltabox/toolchain/config';

// Discover + validate a config (JSON, CJS, ESM or TypeScript).
const loaded = await loadConfig({ packageJsonKeys: ['myapp'], schema });

// Or parse a specific source.
const fromEnv = parseEnvConfig(schema, process.env, { envPrefix: 'MYAPP_' });
const fromCli = parseCliConfig(schema, process.argv.slice(2));
const fromFile = parseConfig(schema, loaded?.config);

// Scaffold a starter config file.
createConfigFile({ name: 'myapp.config.ts', content: '{ enabled: true }' });
```

The loader also accepts the same tsconfig, ancestor and filter options as the
built-in one:

```ts
const loaded = await loadConfig({
    parser: schema,
    configFileOptions: {
        filename: 'myapp.config',
        commonLocation: [{ path: '.' }, { cwd: 'packages', path: '*/' }],
        // Resolve TS imports through this tsconfig (`false` disables it).
        tsconfig: 'tsconfig.loader.json',
        // Search ancestors when nothing is found at cwd (stops at `.git`).
        parent: true,
        // Skip files that are not valid candidates for this loader.
        accept: file => !file.endsWith('.shim.ts'),
    },
});
```

The object API accepts `tsconfig`, `parent` and `accept` directly instead of
nesting them in `configFileOptions`. `findConfigFile` and
`findParentConfigFile` run the same discovery without loading anything.

Discovery defaults to `.`, `config` and `configs`, matching the built-in loader.
`commonLocation.path` globs support `*`, `**`, `?`, simple `[...]` character
classes and `{a,b}` alternatives. A function export is resolved when a
`parser`/`schema` is passed; without one the raw export is returned, so a caller
can supply its own environment (as the dbx plugin probe does).

`collect(schema, options)` lists every config leaf (env/CLI metadata) and
accepts `envPrefix`, `include`/`exclude`, `maxDepth`, and `validate` with
`errorOptions` for required/empty values. `loadConfigSync` handles JSON and
CommonJS only; use `loadConfigAsync` (or a custom `loader`) for TypeScript.

### Scaffolding formats

`createConfigFile` infers the format from the file name (or takes an explicit
`type`): `file` (TypeScript/JavaScript `defineConfig`), `json`, `yaml`, `env`
(`KEY=value` lines) and `cli` (`--flag=value` lines). Object `content` is
serialized for the chosen format, and `defaults`/`overrides` merge under/over it:

```ts
createConfigFile({
    name: 'myapp.config.yaml',
    content: { project: { name: 'myapp' } },
    defaults: { project: { license: 'MIT' } },
});

createConfigFile({ name: '.env.example', content: { APP_HOST: 'localhost' } });
```

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/config/logging.md
---
# Logging

Every toolchain message goes through one logger. Configure it in the config:

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        logger: { level: 'debug', color: false, name: 'dbx' },
    },
});
```

| Option     | Values                                             | Default |
| ---------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| `level`    | `debug` | `info` | `warn` | `error` | `silent` | `info`  |
| `color`    | `true` | `false`                                  | `true`  |
| `name`     | prefix for non-indented lines                      | `dbx`   |
| `suppress` | id, message substring or `/regex/` (single/array)  | none    |
| `logger`   | custom `ToolchainLogger` implementation            | none    |

`suppress` silences matching warnings/errors. A string matches an emitted id
exactly or a message substring; a `/pattern/flags` string is treated as a regex.
Ids are rendered in uppercase in the output (eg. `[FMT_CONFLICT]`), but match
the lowercase id when suppressing. It accepts one value or an array:

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
toolchain: {
    logger: {
        suppress: ['fmt.conflict', 'deprecated option', '/^Could not .* globally/'],
    },
}
```

Colour is **on by default** (the toolchain forces it rather than relying on TTY
autodetection); `--no-color` or `logger: { color: false }` turn it off. Human
output is rendered with [`@clack/prompts`](https://bombshell.dev/clack) — level
symbols (`•` info, `◆` success, `▲` warn, `■` error) and a guide.

### Custom logger

Pass any object implementing the agnostic `ToolchainLogger` interface
(`raw`, `rawError`, `write`, `debug`, `info`, `success`, `warn`, `error`) to
`logger.logger`. Level/suppression checks still apply before your methods run.

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
const custom = {
    raw: (message = '') => process.stdout.write(`${message}\n`),
    rawError: (message = '') => process.stderr.write(`${message}\n`),
    write: () => {},
    debug: () => {},
    info: (message = '') => mySink.info(message),
    success: (message = '') => mySink.info(message),
    warn: (message = '') => mySink.warn(message),
    error: (message = '') => mySink.error(message),
};

export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: { logger: { logger: custom } },
});
```

On the CLI, `--log-level <level>` and `--no-color` override the config (see the
[CLI reference](/guide/cli)); `--no-color` also disables the program's configured
help/error colours. Machine output (`--json`) is written unprefixed
through the same logger.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/config/nested-configs.md
---
# Nested configs

A `dbx.config.*` in a **non-root** folder (a workspace, an app, a nested
project) is merged over the nearest ancestor `dbx.config.*` found while walking
up to the repository root (the walk stops at the `.git` boundary, so it never
picks up a config from outside the repo).

The merge is recursive, but **sections are strictly opt-in**:

* **Only a section the nested config explicitly enables/configures is
  inherited.** If the nested config omits `fmt`, `lint`, `biome`, `changelog`,
  `catalogs` or `logger`, that section stays disabled for that project even when
  the root defines it.
* When the nested config **does** opt in, objects are merged key by key and
  leaves (booleans, strings, numbers, arrays) in the child replace the root's
  value. `true` means "enabled with the parent's options"; `false` disables it.
* **Repository/workspace-scoped sections are never inherited**: `ci`, `tsconfig`,
  `loader`, `templates`, `registry`, `watch`, `providers`, and `vite`. A
  workflow, workspace tsconfig tree, config loader, source/registry policy,
  watch process or Vite config describes the repository or one workspace, so a
  child starts without the parent's values for them. In particular, the root
  `tsconfig` task already expands every workspace `tsconfig.json`; inheriting it
  into each workspace would only re-scan that subtree. `loader` is read from the
  nearest config file to import the nested config, but it is not merged into the
  child's config.
* **`project` metadata is the exception**: shared metadata (`author`, `license`,
  `homepage`, `repo`, `packageManager`, ...) is inherited because it is project
  metadata, not a task section.

`vite.fmt` / `vite.lint` are hoisted into the top-level `fmt.oxc` / `lint.oxc`
**when the nested config opts into `fmt` / `lint`**.

```ts [<root>/dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        logger: { level: 'debug', color: false },
        fmt: { oxc: { printWidth: 100, singleQuote: true } },
        vite: { shim: 'static', resolve: { tsconfigPaths: true } },
    },
});

// <root>/packages/web/dbx.config.ts — opts into `fmt` + `logger`; `vite` is local
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        logger: { level: 'warn' }, // opts in; leaf overrides the root's level
        fmt: true, // opts in; inherits the root's `fmt` options
        vite: {
            shim: 'static',
            resolve: { tsconfigPaths: true },
            run: { tasks: { build: { command: 'vp pack' } } },
        },
    },
});
```

The workspace above ends up with `logger: { level: 'warn', color: false }` and
the root's `fmt` options (because it opted in with `fmt: true`). If it omitted
`fmt`, it would have no `fmt` section at all. Its `vite.run` holds only the
`build` task it declares — the root's tasks are not merged in.

> **`vite` is never inherited.** A workspace only has the `vite` config it
> declares itself; a project with no `vite` section keeps its hand-written
> `vite.config.*` alone. Declare the settings it needs (`shim`, `resolve`,
> `plugins`, ...) in its own config. `vite.fmt` / `vite.lint` are hoisted into
> `fmt` / `lint` only when the workspace opts into those sections.

> **Arrays replace, so repeat what you need.** If a workspace opts into `fmt`
> and sets `fmt.oxc.ignorePatterns`, that array replaces the root's list (it is
> not appended). Either keep the root patterns in the workspace array, or put
> the shared pattern on the root config — for example `**/vite.config.ts` there
> covers every workspace's generated shim.

> **`project` is inherited except its identity fields.** `name`, `scope`,
> `description` and `type` are per-project, so a non-root config keeps its own (or
> falls back to its `package.json`) and is still detected from its own files — a
> root `project` never renames a workspace. The shared fields (`author`,
> `license`, `homepage`, `repo`, `packageManager`, ...) flow down so their
> `package.json` values and replacement tokens stay shared.
> `project: { inherit: false }` disables project inheritance entirely. `hooks`
> are not inherited either — a parent's hooks are code and do not run for a
> nested project's sync.

## Configless projects

A project with **no `dbx.config.*` of its own** is not managed by the toolchain
by default: it does not inherit the ancestor config, `dbx sync` leaves it
alone, and its files are never generated or pruned. This avoids surprising
changes in packages that never opted in.

To manage configless projects, opt in explicitly:

* **Config:** set `toolchain.project.manageConfigless: true` on the ancestor
  config (it is repository-scoped, so a configless project inherits the choice
  through the parent config).
* **CLI:** pass `dbx sync --configless` (or `dbx watch --configless`).
* **VS Code:** enable `deltabox.toolchain.manageConfigless`.

```ts [<root>/dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        project: {
            manageConfigless: true,
        },
    },
});
```

When enabled, a configless project inherits the ancestor config (the configless
opt-in is the explicit opt-in for the whole project; repository-scoped sections
are still dropped) and `dbx sync` regenerates its managed files.

> Configless projects are still **discovered** (so the Projects view and the
> project graph can show them); they are just not managed until you opt in.

## Vite plugin mode

A project can also be configured by the `dbx()` Vite plugin instead of a
`dbx.config.*`:

```ts [vite.config.ts]
import { defineConfig } from 'vite-plus';

import { dbx } from '@deltabox/toolchain/vite';

export default defineConfig({
    plugins: [dbx({ toolchain: { project: { name: 'app' }, fmt: { oxc: true } } })],
});
```

The loader evaluates `vite.config.*` and reads the plugin options, so the CLI,
sync, watch and the VS Code extension all see the config with no
`dbx.config.*`. When both exist, the `dbx.config.*` is the base and the plugin
options are merged on top (the plugin layer keeps the sections it does not
mention). In plugin mode the toolchain never writes or manages
`vite.config.*`, and it watches the plugin config for changes.

In a **workspace** plugin config, leave `fmt` and `lint` out: the root
`vite.config.*` already owns them, and Vite+ applies the root options (including
its `ignorePatterns`) to the workspace. Declaring `fmt: true` / `lint: true`
there would select the shared defaults instead and shadow the root config.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/config/opt-in-by-presence.md
---
# Opt-in by presence

Every section under `toolchain` is **opt-in by presence**: the toolchain only
touches an area you actually ask for.

* Omit a section — that area is left completely alone.
* `section: true` — enable it with defaults (when the section has defaults).
* `section: false` — explicitly disable it.
* `section: { ...options }` — enable and configure it.

This applies to nested sections too. `ci` is opt-in, and every workflow inside it
(`ci.ci`, `ci.release`, `ci.issues`, `ci.changelog`, `ci.sync`) is opt-in as
well: omit a workflow (or set it to `false`) and the toolchain will not generate
or manage its file. Setting `ci: false` or `ci: { enabled: false }` disables the
whole section, including every nested workflow and the changelog pipeline.

The same rule backs `ci.changelog`: it is only managed when you declare it, and
`ci.changelog: false` (or `enabled: false`) disables both its workflow and the
changelog pipeline.

Helpers `sectionEnabled(section)` and `sectionConfig(section)` implement this and
are exported for programmatic use.

The top-level `changelog` section configures the manual pipeline for `dbx
changelog`/the API. It does not enable CI by itself; `ci.changelog` inherits its
options when they are not overridden. See
[Manual `toolchain.changelog`](/guide/changelog/#manual-toolchainchangelog).

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/config/programmatic-api.md
---
# Programmatic config API

```ts
import { loadToolchainConfig, runSync, defaultSyncTasks } from '@deltabox/toolchain';

const { config, tokens, projectType } = await loadToolchainConfig(process.cwd());
await runSync({ tasks: defaultSyncTasks(), cwd: process.cwd(), config, tokens, projectType });
```

`loadToolchainConfig` accepts `loaderTsconfig` to override the tsconfig used to
import the config (the same option as [`toolchain.loader.tsconfig`](/guide/config/loader)):

```ts
const loaded = await loadToolchainConfig(process.cwd(), {
    loaderTsconfig: 'tsconfig.loader.json', // or false
});
```

The result also reports `configless` and `managed`, which tell whether the
project has no config of its own and whether the toolchain should manage it.

Full section reference: [dbx.config](/config/reference).

url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/config/providers.md
---
# Provider config

Provider passthrough commands (Vite+) follow the logger's colour setting. The
`providers` section can force provider colours on or off on its own:

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        providers: { color: false },
    },
});
```

| Option  | Values            | Default        |
| ------- | ----------------- | -------------- |
| `color` | `true` | `false` | inherit logger |

`color: false` runs the wrapped binary with `NO_COLOR=1` and `FORCE_COLOR=0`, so
it emits plain output even on a colour terminal. The global CLI `--no-color`
flag turns provider colour off too. See [Providers](/guide/providers#colour).

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/config/vite.md
---
# Vite+ config

The whole Vite+ config lives in `toolchain.vite`. Every key is passed through
verbatim to Vite+, so `dbx.config.*` stays the only hand-authored root config:

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        vite: {
            test: { include: ['src/**/*.test.ts'], environment: 'node' },
            lint: { ignorePatterns: ['dist/**'] },
            fmt: { semi: true, singleQuote: true },
        },
    },
});
```

`dbx sync` writes a thin root `vite.config.ts` that resolves that config at load
time, so the generated file never duplicates (or drifts from) `dbx.config.*`:

```ts [vite.config.ts]
import { defineConfig, type ViteUserConfig } from 'vite-plus';

// Generated by @deltabox/toolchain — edit the vite section in dbx.config and run `dbx sync`.
import { resolveVite } from '@deltabox/toolchain/vite';

export default defineConfig(resolveVite<ViteUserConfig>({ cwd: import.meta.dirname }));
```

The shim imports `defineConfig` from whichever Vite package the project installs
(`vite` or `vite-plus`, detected from `package.json`), so a plain `vite` project
gets `import { defineConfig, type UserConfig } from 'vite'` and
`resolveVite<UserConfig>(...)`.

`resolveVite(options?)` resolves the **same-directory** `dbx.config.*` (so a
nested `vite.config.ts` uses the nested config it sits next to), or the
`toolchain` you pass, then returns `toolchain.vite`. Pass `vite` inline to merge
overrides over the loaded section (`resolveVite({ vite: { ... } })`). It is
exported from `@deltabox/toolchain/vite` for programmatic use too.

The single toolchain opt-out is `config`. Set `vite: { config: false }` to leave
a hand-written `vite.config.ts` alone; set `config` to a string (relative to the
project, or absolute) to write the managed shim at a different path instead.
Everything else under `vite` is Vite+ config (plugins, `test`, `lint`, `fmt`,
`run.tasks`, ...), so `toolchain.vite` is the full Vite+ configuration. The section is typed as Vite+'s own config
(`ToolchainViteConfig` = Vite's `UserConfig` as augmented by Vite+), so the whole
Vite+ surface autocompletes in `dbx.config.ts`.

### Nested workspaces

`vite` is **never inherited**. A workspace only has the `vite` config it
declares itself; a project with no `vite` section keeps its hand-written
`vite.config.*` untouched. Declare the settings the workspace needs in its own
config:

```ts [packages/web/dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        vite: {
            shim: 'static',
            resolve: { tsconfigPaths: true },
            run: { tasks: { build: { command: 'vp pack' } } },
        },
    },
});
```

`vite.fmt` / `vite.lint` are the exception: when the workspace **opts into
`fmt` / `lint`**, they are hoisted into the top-level `fmt.oxc` / `lint.oxc`
before inheritance, so shared formatter/linter settings flow down.

### Static shims

By default the shim calls `resolveVite` at load time (`shim: 'runtime'`). Set
`vite: { shim: 'static' }` to serialize the resolved config into the shim
instead:

```ts [vite.config.ts]
import { defineConfig, type ViteUserConfig } from 'vite-plus';

export default defineConfig<ViteUserConfig>({
    resolve: { tsconfigPaths: true },
    run: { tasks: {/* ... */} },
});
```

A static shim imports only `defineConfig`, so Vite+ can load it without a built
`@deltabox/toolchain` (useful for source-first monorepos and bootstrapping). It
must stay serializable: functions, regexps and class instances are rejected at
sync time (plugins still work with `shim: 'runtime'`).

Runtime shims import `@deltabox/toolchain/vite` by default. Set
`vite.shimImport` to change that specifier, for example to a local wrapper that
re-exports `resolveVite`. Relative values are resolved from the repository root
and rewritten relative to each generated config:

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        vite: {
            shimImport: './scripts/local-vite-resolver.ts',
        },
    },
});
```

This only affects `shim: 'runtime'` (the default); static shims have no
toolchain import.

Vite 8 resolves TypeScript `paths` through `resolve.tsconfigPaths`. Set it in
`toolchain.vite.resolve` (and in Vitest configs) to reuse the tsconfig aliases:

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        vite: { resolve: { tsconfigPaths: true } },
    },
});
```

For explicit aliases (or Vite versions without built-in `paths` support), use
`resolveTsconfig()` from `@deltabox/toolchain/tsconfig` (see the
[tsconfig guide](/guide/tsconfig#resolving-a-tsconfig)).

Add the shim to `vite.fmt.ignorePatterns` so Oxfmt leaves the generated file
alone - without it `vp fmt` would rewrite the shim and `dbx sync --check` would
report drift. In a monorepo put `**/vite.config.ts` on the root config: workspace
`fmt` settings are inherited, but a workspace's `ignorePatterns` array replaces
the root's list. The default fmt ignores already include `**/vite.config.ts`;
`dbx migrate --from vite` adds `/vite.config.ts` to `vite.fmt` only when the
folded config already owns `fmt`.

## Format and lint defaults

Opt in with `vite: { fmt: true }` / `vite: { lint: true }` to use the toolchain
defaults (`DEFAULT_FMT_RULES` / `DEFAULT_LINT_RULES`, exported from
`@deltabox/toolchain`). An options object is merged over those defaults, so
`fmt: { semi: false }` keeps the shared ignores and print width and only changes
`semi`. Shared ignore lists live in `DEFAULT_FMT_IGNORE_PATTERNS` /
`DEFAULT_LINT_IGNORE_PATTERNS`, both layered over `DEFAULT_IGNORE_PATTERNS`.
All three are exported (readonly) from `@deltabox/toolchain` and
`@deltabox/toolchain/shared`, so you can compose your own list instead of
repeating the defaults:

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
import { DEFAULT_FMT_IGNORE_PATTERNS, defineConfig } from '@deltabox/toolchain';

export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        vite: {
            fmt: {
                ignorePatterns: [...DEFAULT_FMT_IGNORE_PATTERNS, '**/fixtures/**'],
            },
        },
    },
});
```

Import sorting is enabled by default too. `sortImports` uses the usual groups
(`builtin`, `external`, `internal`/`subpath`, relatives, styles) plus a
`workspace` group whose patterns come from every `dbx.config.*` project in the
repository, so consumer packages sort together without a hand-written
`customGroups` entry. Override `sortImports: false` to disable it, or set your
own groups — the resolved workspace group is still appended (and listed in
`groups`) unless you disable sorting.

To reuse the workspace group in your own `sortImports`, import the resolver:

```ts
import { resolveFmtCustomGroups } from '@deltabox/toolchain';

const customGroups = await resolveFmtCustomGroups();
// [{ groupName: 'workspace', elementNamePattern: ['@org/**', 'app', 'app/**', ...] }]
```

`resolveFmtCustomGroups()` reads the project graph, so it is safe to call from
inside `dbx.config.*`. Pass `{ config: 'path/to/dbx.config.ts' }` to resolve a
specific config instead of the discovered one, or an inline `project` to add a
project the graph does not know about.

In VS Code, set `deltabox.toolchain.enableFormatImportGroupDefaults` to `false`
(user or workspace settings) to stop the extension from adding the workspace
group.

## Oxc config files

Vite+ reads `fmt`/`lint` from `vite.config.ts`, but the Oxc VS Code extension
reads `.oxfmtrc.json` / `.oxlintrc.json`. When `vite.fmt` / `vite.lint` are
defined, `dbx sync` writes those files as managed files so the editor picks up
the same configuration. Only the root gets them by default; a nested
`dbx.config.*` gets its own pair only when it defines `vite.fmt` / `vite.lint`
itself (an inherited root config does not create per-workspace files).

To adopt an existing hand-written `vite.config.ts`, fold it in with the
migration (see [Migrations](/guide/migrations/#vite-config)):

```sh
dbx migrate --from vite --write   # folds the object into toolchain.vite (routes fmt/lint)
dbx sync                          # writes the managed vite.config.ts shim
```

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/monorepo.md
---
# Monorepo guide

## Project graph

`dbx projects` discovers every workspace package and writes a
dependency graph to `.dbx/toolchain/projects.json`. The VS Code extension and the
`sync --recursive` command consume it.

## tsconfig generation

Enable the `tsconfig` section and the toolchain generates each workspace's
`tsconfig.json` (extending `tsconfig.default.json`) and, for a monorepo root, a
`tsconfig.workspaces.json` wiring project references and path aliases:

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        project: { type: 'monorepo-root', name: 'myapp', scope: '@org' },
        tsconfig: { refs: true, aliases: true, indent: 4 },
    },
});
```

See the [tsconfig guide](/guide/tsconfig) for every option and why the toolchain
splits the config across several files.

## Scaffolding a monorepo

```sh
dbx project:init:monorepo --name myapp --scope @org --out .
dbx project:init:workspace --name utils --scope @org --root . --dir packages/utils
```

## Tasks

`deltabox toolchain` (and Vite+ consumers) use **Vite Task** (`vp run`, exposed
as `dbx run`) instead of Turbo. The package graph orders execution via each
package's `package.json` dependencies.

Run tasks from the workspace root. `vp run -r <task>` runs every package's task
in dependency order; `vp run --filter ./apps/web <task>` narrows it. For the
built-in app commands, Vite+ resolves the target package from the root and prints
the direct `vp -C <dir> <command>` form, so you never need to `cd` between
packages. Use `-C` when a command must behave as if it ran inside a package.
To always target one app from the root, set `defaultPackage: './apps/web'`
(a per-command object also works) in the root `vite.config.ts`.

Each package can declare `build`, `typecheck` and `test` in its own
`vite.config.ts` `run.tasks` (or in `dbx.config.ts` under `toolchain.vite`) with
explicit cache input/output, so `vp run` reports cache hits (a `package.json`
script cannot carry cache config). Use `vp pack` / `vp test` instead of the
individual `tsdown` / `vitest` binaries:

```ts [packages/<pkg>/vite.config.ts]
import { defineConfig } from 'vite-plus';

export default defineConfig({
    run: {
        tasks: {
            build: {
                command: 'vp pack',
                cache: {
                    input: [{ auto: true }, '!dist/**', '!**/*.tsbuildinfo'],
                    output: ['dist/**'],
                },
            },
            typecheck: {
                command: 'tsc -p tsconfig.build.json --noEmit',
                cache: { input: [{ auto: true }, '!**/*.tsbuildinfo'], output: [] },
            },
            test: {
                command: 'vp test run',
                cache: { input: [{ auto: true }, '!**/*.tsbuildinfo'], output: [] },
            },
        },
    },
});
```

The root `package.json` orchestrates them and adds the umbrella build:

```json [package.json]
{
    "scripts": {
        "build": "dbx run --filter \"./packages/*\" build && dbx run build:root",
        "test": "dbx run --filter \"./packages/*\" test && dbx run test:root"
    }
}
```

`dbx run --filter "./packages/*" build` runs each package's `build` in
dependency order (excluding the root, which avoids recursion), then `build:root`
builds the umbrella dist.

## Shared formatting and linting

Define `fmt` and `lint` once in the root `vite.config.ts`, and run `vp fmt`,
`vp lint` and `vp check` from the root. Vite+ does not apply nested configs to
individual files, and `vp check` always uses the root blocks, so package-level
`fmt` / `lint` blocks are not recommended. Use `overrides` for package- or
file-specific settings:

```ts [vite.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    lint: {
        overrides: [
            { files: ['apps/api/**'], env: { node: true } },
            { files: ['**/*.test.ts'], plugins: ['vitest'] },
        ],
    },
    fmt: {
        overrides: [{ files: ['**/*.md'], options: { proseWrap: 'always' } }],
    },
});
```

Globs resolve from the root config, so use workspace paths such as
`apps/web/**`; do not add per-package formatter/linter blocks.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/project.md
---
# Project

The `project` section is a package's **canonical metadata**. It is the single
place to declare who a package is, and it does three jobs:

1. **Defines `package.json` fields.** On `dbx sync`, the fields the section
   defines are written into the project's `package.json` (everything else is left
   untouched).
2. **Feeds the {{ token }} replacements.** Every template (`biome.json`,
   workflows, tsconfigs, READMEs, ...) reads these values.
3. **Drives scaffolding.** `dbx project:init*` uses the section as its defaults
   (and `project.type` picks the kind of project to generate).

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        project: {
            type: 'monorepo-root',
            name: 'myapp',
            scope: '@org',
            author: 'Myapp Inc. <hello@myapp.dev>',
            license: 'MIT',
            homepage: 'https://myapp.dev',
            repo: 'https://github.com/myapp/myapp',
            description: 'The myapp monorepo',
            nodeVersion: '22',
            packageManager: 'yarn',
            packageManagerVersion: '4.17.1',
        },
    },
});
```

## `package.json` mapping

A sync writes only the fields the config **defines**; a field you omit is never
touched. The mapping:

| `project` field  | `package.json` field | Notes                                              |
| ---------------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `name` + `scope` | `name`               | `@org/app` when a scope is set, else `app`.        |
| `description`    | `description`        |                                                    |
| `author`         | `author`             |                                                    |
| `license`        | `license`            |                                                    |
| `homepage`       | `homepage`           |                                                    |
| `repo`           | `repository`         | `{ type: 'git', url }` (+ `directory`, see below). |
| `packageManager` | `packageManager`     | `yarn@4.17.1` when `packageManagerVersion` is set. |
| `type`           | —                    | Project kind for detection/scaffolding.            |
| `nodeVersion`    | —                    | Node version for CI/templates (not `engines`).     |

`nodeVersion` is intentionally **not** written to `engines`: it is the Node
version the generated workflows run on (`node-version: '{{nodeVersion}}'`), which
is a different concern from the published `engines.node` range.

## Workspace inheritance

A non-root `dbx.config.*` is merged over the nearest ancestor config (see
[Configuration → Nested configs](/guide/config/nested-configs)). Tooling
sections are strictly opt-in for nested configs; `project` metadata is the
exception because it is metadata, not a task section. For `project`
specifically:

* **Identity fields are never inherited**: `name`, `scope`, `description` and
  `type` are per-project. A workspace keeps its own values, falling back to its
  `package.json` for `name`/`scope`/`description`, and is still detected from its
  own files — a root `project` never renames or rescopes a workspace. The scope
  therefore comes from the workspace's own `package.json` name (eg.
  `@org/web`); an unscoped name stays unscoped unless the workspace config sets
  `scope`.
* **Shared metadata is inherited** (`author`, `license`, `homepage`, `repo`,
  `packageManager`, ...), so those `package.json` values and replacement tokens
  stay shared.
* **`inherit: false`** opts out entirely: the project keeps only its own `project`
  and ignores the parent's (useful for an unrelated package inside the tree).
* **`manageConfigless: true`** opts into managing projects that have no
  `dbx.config.*` of their own. It is repository-scoped (set it on the root
  config) and is **disabled by default**: configless projects are discovered
  but never synced or generated for unless you opt in. See
  [Configless projects](/guide/config/nested-configs#configless-projects).

```ts [packages/web/dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        // `name`/`scope` are identity; here the scope comes from the package's
        // `@org/web` name. `author`/`license`/`repo` still inherit from the root.
        project: { name: 'web' },
        // ...
    },
});
```

### `repo` resolves to the workspace path

For a non-root project, `repo` also resolves to the workspace's location in the
repository, written as `repository.directory`:

```json [package.json]
{
    "repository": {
        "type": "git",
        "url": "https://github.com/myapp/myapp",
        "directory": "packages/web"
    }
}
```

The directory is computed relative to the repository root (the nearest ancestor
with a `.git`), exactly like npm expects for a monorepo workspace.

## When the section is absent

If `project` is not defined, nothing is written to `package.json` — and the
replacement tokens fall back to the project's **own `package.json`** values
(`name`/`scope` from `name`, plus `description`, `author`, `license`, `homepage`,
`repository`, `engines.node`, `packageManager`). So a repo with no `project`
section still generates correct tokens from its existing metadata.

## Scaffolding

`dbx project:init`, `dbx project:init:monorepo` and
`dbx project:init:workspace` read `project` as their defaults, and:

* **`name`** comes from `--name`, or from `project.name` when the scaffold writes
  **into** the current project. A scaffold `--out` elsewhere never inherits the
  parent project's name — it uses the target directory's basename instead (pass
  `--name` to override). A workspace always needs an explicit `--name` (the
  root's name is not the workspace name).
* **`--type` must be valid** (`project`, `monorepo-root` or `monorepo-workspace`)
  when passed explicitly; an invalid value is rejected. A `project.type` in the
  config still drives `dbx sync` detection, but scaffolding deliberately ignores
  it (a scaffold launched from a monorepo root must not tag a workspace with the
  root's type).

```sh
dbx project:init --name my-app --scope @org --type project --out ./my-app
dbx project:init:monorepo --name myapp --scope @org --out .
dbx project:init:monorepo --name myapp --scope @org --example --out .
dbx project:init:workspace --name web --root . --dir packages/web
```

The scaffolded `dbx.config.ts` spells the resolved `project` fields out, so a
generated project is self-describing from day one. Existing files in the output
directory are never overwritten (pass `--force` to replace them), and a scaffold
refuses to write outside its output directory.

A nested `project:init` below a root that already has `.oxfmtrc.json` /
`.oxlintrc.json` skips its own Oxc files and `fmt.oxc` / `lint.oxc` opt-ins, so it
uses the root formatting/linting setup.

Pass `--package-manager <pm>` (`yarn` default, or `pnpm` / `npm` / `bun`) to
choose the manager the scaffold targets.

## Package manager and catalogs

The scaffold and `dbx sync` write a **catalog** (`package -> version range`) into
the file the package manager reads it from, so dependencies can be declared with
`catalog:`:

| Manager | Catalog file          | Notes                                        |
| ------- | --------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `yarn`  | `.yarnrc.yml`         | `catalog:` / `catalogs:` (default + named).  |
| `pnpm`  | `pnpm-workspace.yaml` | `catalog:` / `catalogs:`.                    |
| `bun`   | `package.json`        | `workspaces.catalog`.                        |
| `npm`   | —                     | No catalog support; dependencies are pinned. |

Scaffolding resolves the manager from the `packageManager` input, writes the
catalog of the packages the project depends on, and **opts into it in the
generated `dbx.config.*`**, so `dbx sync` owns the file. To manage catalogs in an
existing project, add a `catalogs` section (see
[Package catalogs](/guide/catalogs)):

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        project: { packageManager: 'yarn' },
        catalogs: {
            packages: { react: '^19.0.0', lodash: '^4.17.21' },
            named: { legacy: { react: '^18.0.0' } },
        },
    },
});
```

`dbx sync` writes (and keeps in sync) `catalog:` / `catalogs:` in `.yarnrc.yml`
(Yarn) or `pnpm-workspace.yaml` (pnpm). A catalog file is only written when it is
absent or already toolchain-managed (it carries a marker comment); a hand-written
one is left untouched. Bun catalogs live in `package.json` and npm has no catalog
support — both emit a warning.

## Programmatic API

```ts
import { projectFromPackageJson, projectToPackageJson, projectSyncTask } from '@deltabox/toolchain';

// Seed a config from an existing package.json.
const project = projectFromPackageJson(require('./package.json'));

// Map the defined fields onto package.json fields.
const pkgFields = projectToPackageJson(project, { directory: 'packages/web' });

// The sync task itself.
projectSyncTask();
```

| Export                        | Description                                                         |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `projectFromPackageJson(pkg)` | Derive project metadata from a `package.json`.                      |
| `projectToPackageJson(p, o?)` | Map defined project fields onto `package.json` fields.              |
| `projectSyncTask()`           | The sync task that applies the `project` section to `package.json`. |
