---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/formatting.md
---
# Formatting & linting

`toolchain.fmt` and `toolchain.lint` select a formatter/linter, hold its
options, and optionally add project-scoped VS Code defaults:

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        fmt: {
            vscode: true, // add missing VS Code formatter settings (default false)
            oxc: { printWidth: 100, singleQuote: true },
            biome: { formatter: { indentWidth: 4 } },
        },
        lint: {
            vscode: true,
            oxc: { rules: { eqeqeq: 'warn' } },
            eslint: { rules: {} },
        },
    },
});
```

The supported tools are:

* `fmt`: `oxc` (Oxfmt), `biome`, `prettier`, `dprint`.
* `lint`: `oxc` (Oxlint), `biome`, `eslint`.

Each tool accepts `true` (use the defaults) or `false` (disable that tool), in
addition to its options object. The Oxfmt/Oxlint option types are generated from
the tools' official JSON schemas (vendored in the package), so editor completion
and the generated config reference match the tool.

The shared ignore lists are exported from `@deltabox/toolchain` and
`@deltabox/toolchain/shared`: `DEFAULT_IGNORE_PATTERNS` (build/cache dirs), and
`DEFAULT_FMT_IGNORE_PATTERNS` / `DEFAULT_LINT_IGNORE_PATTERNS` (the Oxc defaults,
layered over `DEFAULT_IGNORE_PATTERNS`). Import them to extend the defaults
rather than re-listing them.

Oxfmt import sorting is enabled in the defaults as well. `sortImports` includes
a `workspace` group built from every `dbx.config.*` project's scope/name;
`resolveFmtCustomGroups()` returns that group so you can reuse it in a custom
`sortImports` config. Set `sortImports: false` to opt out.

## Shorthand opt-in

`fmt: true` / `lint: true` (or an options object with only `vscode`) picks a tool
automatically. `dbx sync` resolves it in this order:

1. the project's `.vscode/settings.json`;
2. the nearest `package.json` or tooling config file, walking up to the repo
   root (a workspace-specific tool beats a root-installed one);
3. the VS Code user settings language blocks;
4. the Oxc defaults.

Each level prefers a tool's own config file (`.oxfmtrc.json`, `biome.json`,
`.prettierrc`, `dprint.json`, `.eslintrc.*`, ...) before its `package.json`
dependency, and honours the formatter/linter precedence. If nothing is found,
sync warns (`fmt.no-tool` / `lint.no-tool`) and still applies the Oxc defaults.

Existing user-owned config files are not overwritten blindly: the detected
tool's options are read into the matching `toolchain.fmt.*` /
`toolchain.lint.*` entry. Oxc options are merged over the toolchain defaults
using the same mapping as [`dbx migrate`](/guide/migrations/).

## Running the active tool

`dbx fmt` / `dbx lint` run the tool the config (or discovery) selects, even when
`toolchain.fmt` / `toolchain.lint` is omitted:

* an explicit `toolchain.fmt.*` / `toolchain.lint.*` tool wins, in precedence
  order;
* otherwise the same discovery `dbx sync` uses picks a tool from the project
  `.vscode/settings.json`, the nearest config file/`package.json`, or the VS
  Code user settings;
* with nothing configured or installed, they fall back to `vp fmt` / `vp lint`
  (Oxfmt / Oxlint).

Mode flags are translated per tool (`--check`/`--write` for formatters, `--fix`
for linters) and other operands are forwarded. Oxc keeps the full Vite+
passthrough, so `dbx vite fmt ...` still accepts every `vp` flag.

## Formatting managed files

Managed-file formatting is **opt-in**. Enable `sync.format` to format the files
`dbx sync` writes with the project's active formatter, in fix mode. This keeps
generated files (workflows, tsconfigs, editor settings, configs, ...) consistent
with the rest of the repository instead of leaving them in the generator's raw
output.

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
toolchain: {
    sync: {
        format: {
            enabled: true,
            fix: true,       // default; false runs the formatter in check mode
            command: 'prettier --write {files}', // optional override
            exclude: ['**/generated/**'],        // per-file opt-out
        },
    },
}
```

`sync.format: true` uses the defaults (enabled + fix). It is disabled when the
section/key is absent; `sync.format: false` disables it explicitly.

The default command follows the detected/configured formatter:

| Tool             | Fix mode                       | Check mode (`fix: false`)  |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------ | -------------------------- |
| Vite+ Oxfmt      | `vp fmt <files>`               | `vp fmt --check <files>`   |
| standalone Oxfmt | `oxfmt <files>`                | `oxfmt --check <files>`    |
| Prettier         | `prettier --write <files>`     | `prettier --check <files>` |
| Biome            | `biome format --write <files>` | `biome format <files>`     |
| dprint           | `dprint fmt <files>`           | `dprint check <files>`     |

A custom `command` is split like a shell command line (quotes are honoured). The
`{files}` token expands to the managed files; when it is absent, the files are
appended. If no formatter can be detected, the step is skipped.

The same switch is available on the command line and in VS Code:

```sh
dbx sync --no-format                    # disable for this run
dbx sync --no-format-fix                # run the formatter in check mode
dbx sync --format-command "prettier --write {files}"
dbx sync --format-exclude "**/generated/**"
```

VS Code exposes them as `deltabox.toolchain.formatManagedFiles`,
`formatManagedFilesFix`, `formatManagedFilesCommand` and
`formatManagedFilesExclude`.

`dbx sync --check` temporarily writes + formats the files to compare the same
content a real sync would produce, then restores the originals; a successful
check therefore reflects the formatted output too.

## Precedence

When more than one formatter/linter is configured, editor defaults use:

* **formatters**: `oxc` > `biome` > `prettier` > `dprint`.
* **linters**: `oxc` > `biome` > `eslint`.

`dbx sync` warns (`fmt.conflict` / `lint.conflict`) when this happens; silence it
with [`logger.suppress`](/guide/config/logging).

`toolchain.vite.fmt` / `toolchain.vite.lint` are the Oxc config written by Vite+,
and **override** `fmt.oxc` / `lint.oxc` with a deep merge (scalars, arrays and
booleans in `vite.*` win). With both:

```ts
toolchain: {
    fmt: { oxc: { semi: false, singleQuote: true } },
    vite: { fmt: { singleQuote: false } },
}
// effective Oxfmt options: { semi: false, singleQuote: false }
```

## Generated config files

* `fmt.oxc` / `lint.oxc` (+ `vite.fmt` / `vite.lint`) write managed
  `.oxfmtrc.json` / `.oxlintrc.json`.
* `fmt.biome` / `lint.biome` merge into the managed `biome.json`.
* The deprecated top-level `biome` section still works; prefer
  `fmt.biome` / `lint.biome`.

Oxc files are root-only unless a nested `dbx.config.*` defines `fmt.oxc` /
`lint.oxc` / `vite.fmt` / `vite.lint` itself. Biome keeps its existing
per-project behaviour.

When more than one formatter or linter is configured, sync warns (`fmt.conflict`
/ `lint.conflict`) because the generated config files and editor defaults may
conflict.

## VS Code editor defaults

Set `fmt.vscode` and/or `lint.vscode` (both default `false`) to add missing
project-scoped settings to `.vscode/settings.json`. The generated defaults are
deliberately small:

* `editor.defaultFormatter`
* language blocks (`[javascript]`, `[typescript]`, ...)
* `editor.codeActionsOnSave` (lint only)

Use an options object to override or exclude individual keys:

```ts
toolchain: {
    fmt: {
        oxc: {},
        vscode: {
            overrides: {
                'editor.defaultFormatter': 'oxc.oxc-vscode',
                '[typescript]': { 'editor.defaultFormatter': 'esbenp.prettier-vscode' },
            },
            exclude: ['[javascript]'],
        },
    },
    lint: { oxc: {}, vscode: true },
}
```

These editor defaults are **not tracked** and existing keys are never
overridden. (The separate Conventional Commits/Biome VS Code sync may track
`.vscode/settings.json` when those sections are enabled.) Remove or change the
generated keys freely. Setting `vscode: false` (or omitting it) adds nothing.

A nested project scaffolded below a root that already has `.oxfmtrc.json` /
`.oxlintrc.json` omits its own Oxc files and `fmt.oxc` / `lint.oxc` opt-ins, so
`dbx fmt` / `dbx lint` keep using the root configuration.

## Migrating

```sh
dbx migrate --from oxc --write        # .oxfmtrc/.oxlintrc -> fmt.oxc/lint.oxc
dbx migrate --from biome --from prettier --write
dbx migrate --from all --write
```

Unless `--target` is given, the migrated formatter/linter options go to
`toolchain.vite.fmt`/`toolchain.vite.lint` when the existing Vite config already
defines `fmt`/`lint`; otherwise they go to the top-level
`toolchain.fmt.oxc`/`toolchain.lint.oxc`. See [Migrations](/guide/migrations/).

## Biome

> **Deprecated:** prefer `toolchain.fmt.biome` / `toolchain.lint.biome` (see
> above). The top-level `biome` section still works and still writes
> `biome.json`.

The `biome` section generates a `biome.json` for consumers that still want a
Biome config. The toolchain itself is built on **Oxc** (Oxfmt + Oxlint) through
Vite+, but a repo that runs Biome directly can let the toolchain manage its
`biome.json` from the same `dbx.config.*`.

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        biome: true, // or { overrides: { ... } }
    },
});
```

`dbx sync` writes `biome.json`, resolving the {{ name }} / {{ scope }}
replacement tokens and merging your overrides over the defaults.

If any other formatter/linter is also configured, sync still writes both the
Biome and Oxc config files, but warns (`fmt.conflict` / `lint.conflict`) that the
two tools may conflict. Silencing it is possible with
`logger: { suppress: ['fmt.conflict'] }`; prefer one toolchain per repo.

### Options

| Option      | Type                      | Default              | Description                                  |
| ----------- | ------------------------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `enabled`   | `boolean`                 | enabled when defined | Master switch.                               |
| `vscode`    | `boolean`                 | `true`               | Write the Biome VS Code settings/extensions. |
| `overrides` | `Record<string, unknown>` | —                    | Deep-merged over the generated `biome.json`. |

#### `overrides`

Overrides are merged into the generated config **recursively**, and **arrays are
unioned** (not replaced) — so `files.includes` can be extended:

```ts
biome: {
    overrides: {
        files: { includes: ['!**/generated/**'] },
        formatter: { indentWidth: 2 },
    },
}
```

Default array entries can be pruned with a `$remove:` entry (its value is JSON,
or a raw string when it is not valid JSON) or replaced wholesale with `$reset`:

```ts
import { BIOME_RESET, removeBiomeEntry } from '@deltabox/toolchain/biome';

biome: {
    overrides: {
        files: {
            includes: [
                removeBiomeEntry('!**/.generated'), // drop a default
                '!**/generated/**',
            ],
        },
        assist: {
            actions: {
                source: {
                    organizeImports: {
                        options: { groups: [BIOME_RESET, ['@/lib/**']] },
                    },
                },
            },
        },
    },
}
```

`removeBiomeEntry(entry)` builds the directive, and nested arrays (eg. import
groups) are matched deeply. The same directives work in `fmt.biome` /
`lint.biome`; sources are applied in order, so later ones see earlier results.

#### `vscode`

When on (the default), the sync also writes the recommended Biome VS Code
settings and the Biome extension recommendation (see
[VS Code Extension](/guide/vscode)). Set `biome: { vscode: false }` to skip them.

### Programmatic API

```ts
import {
    BIOME_RESET,
    biomeConfig,
    biomeSyncTask,
    biomeVscodeSettings,
    mergeBiomeConfig,
    removeBiomeEntry,
    renderBiomeConfig,
    renderBiomeJson,
    resolveBiomeArray,
} from '@deltabox/toolchain/biome';
```

| Export                                    | Description                                              |
| ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `biomeSyncTask()`                         | The sync task (writes `biome.json`).                     |
| `biomeConfig` / `biomeVscodeSettings`     | The generic Biome config / recommended VS Code settings. |
| `renderBiomeConfig(tokens, overrides?)`   | Resolve tokens + merge overrides into an object.         |
| `renderBiomeJson(tokens, overrides?)`     | Serialize the rendered config.                           |
| `mergeBiomeConfig(base, patch)`           | The recursive/array-union merge used above.              |
| `resolveBiomeArray(base, patch)`          | Resolve `$remove:`/`$reset` directives for one array.    |
| `removeBiomeEntry(entry)` / `BIOME_RESET` | Build the array-pruning / array-reset directives.        |

> Migrating **from** Biome to Oxc is a different concern — see
> [Migrations](/guide/migrations/).

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/scripts.md
---
# Package scripts

`dbx` writes files, not your `package.json` — but a few scripts are worth
standardizing, because the toolchain's formatting/linting and task running both
go through **Vite+**. Any bare `dbx <command>` that matches a Vite+ command is
forwarded straight to it (`dbx fmt`, `dbx run -r build`, `dbx dev`), so a project
only needs the one `dbx` command. This page shows the recommended root scripts
and how to move an existing Biome + Turbo project onto them.

## Recommended scripts

The repo root `package.json`:

```json [package.json]
{
    "scripts": {
        "fmt": "dbx fmt",
        "lint": "dbx lint --fix",
        "check": "dbx check",
        "build": "dbx run -r build",
        "typecheck": "dbx run -r typecheck",
        "test": "dbx run -r test",
        "dbx:sync": "dbx sync",
        "dbx:watch": "dbx watch",
        "commitlint": "commitlint",
        "postinstall": "vp hooks enable"
    }
}
```

| Script                         | What it does                                                    |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `fmt` / `lint` / `check`       | Oxfmt / Oxlint across the repo (`check` = format check + lint). |
| `build` / `typecheck` / `test` | Runs the task in every workspace, in dependency order.          |
| `dbx:sync` / `dbx:watch`       | Regenerate the managed files / re-sync on change.               |
| `commitlint` / `postinstall`   | Conventional Commits + the Vite+ hook dispatcher.               |

Notes:

* A bare command that names a Vite+ command is forwarded to Vite+ (`vp`) — eg.
  `dbx fmt`, `dbx dev`, `dbx run -r build`, `dbx add zod` (Vite+ aliases too).
  Built-in commands win, so `dbx migrate` is the toolchain's migration — use
  `dbx vite migrate` for Vite+'s. The explicit `dbx vite <command>` passthrough
  always works.
* Vite+ resolves from the **repo root**, so `fmt`/`lint` live there — keep
  them out of the individual workspaces.
* `dbx run -r <task>` runs a task in every workspace package in dependency order.
  A task is either a `package.json` script or a `vite.config.ts` `run.tasks`
  entry. For long-running processes use `dbx run -r --parallel dev`.
* `dbx` is the toolchain binary, so `yarn dbx <cmd>` (eg. `yarn dbx sync`) works
  even without a script; the `dbx:*` aliases are just for discoverability.

When `ci.changelog` is enabled, `dbx sync` writes a `commit-msg` hook that runs
commitlint, so commits are linted locally as well as in CI. On a Vite+ project it
writes the project-owned `.vite-hooks/commit-msg`; activate the dispatcher on
install with `vp hooks enable` (or `vp config`, which also wires agent
integration). Projects without Vite+ keep the husky fallback
(`.husky/commit-msg` with `postinstall: husky`). Hook scripts have no extension,
so on Windows add `.vite-hooks/* text eol=lf` (or the husky equivalent) to
`.gitattributes` — a trailing CR silently breaks the hook.

To check staged files before a commit, add a project-owned
`.vite-hooks/pre-commit` that runs `vp staged`, and configure the checks in the
root `vite.config.ts`:

```ts [vite.config.ts]
staged: {
    '*': 'vp check --fix',
},
```

`vp staged` bundles lint-staged and requires Node.js ≥ 22.22.1 (or ≥ 24.11.0).
`vp hooks enable` only manages the dispatcher; it never overwrites project-owned
hooks such as `commit-msg` and `pre-commit`.

## Vite+ commands with the `dbx()` plugin

When the project uses the `dbx()` Vite plugin (`vite.config.ts`), call Vite+
directly for the toolchain commands:

```json [package.json]
{
    "scripts": {
        "dev": "vp dev",
        "build": "vp build",
        "check": "vp check",
        "test": "vp test",
        "dbx:sync": "dbx sync"
    }
}
```

`vp fmt`, `vp lint`, `vp run -r build` and the rest of the Vite+ commands work
from the repo root; `dbx` still owns `sync`, `watch`, `changelog` and the other
non-Vite+ commands. `dbx fmt` / `dbx lint` remain the portable form — they route
to the detected formatter/linter when a project is not on Vite+.

See Vite+ [Built-in commands vs
scripts](https://viteplus.dev/guide/run#built-in-commands-vs-scripts) for which
commands are built in and which run `package.json` scripts.

## Migrate an existing project

1. Add the toolchain + Vite+, and drop what they replace:

   ```diff
   -    "@biomejs/biome": "catalog:",
   -    "turbo": "^2.11.2",
   +    "@deltabox/toolchain": "^1.2.3",
   +    "vite-plus": "^1.2.0",
   ```

2. Fold the Biome config into a root `vite.config.ts`:

   ```sh
   dbx migrate --from biome --target vite --write
   ```

   Or, if the project uses `dbx.config.ts`, author the Vite+ config there under
   `toolchain.vite`. `dbx sync` then writes the root `vite.config.ts` shim (see
   [Vite+](/guide/config/vite)). `dbx migrate --from vite --write` folds an
   existing hand-written `vite.config.ts` in.

3. Replace the scripts (see the tables below), then delete `biome.json` and
   `turbo.json`.

4. Add a `dbx.config.ts` and sync the managed files:

   ```sh
   dbx sync
   ```

5. Verify — this is what CI runs:

   ```sh
   dbx sync --check
   yarn build
   ```

### Biome → Oxc

| Before                   | After            |
| ------------------------ | ---------------- |
| `biome format --write .` | `dbx fmt`        |
| `biome check --fix .`    | `dbx lint --fix` |
| `biome.json`             | `vite.config.ts` |

Remove `@biomejs/biome`, delete `biome.json`, and drop any per-workspace
`fmt`/`lint` scripts.

### Turbo → Vite Task

| Before            | After                                      |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `turbo build`     | `dbx run -r build`                         |
| `turbo typecheck` | `dbx run -r typecheck`                     |
| `turbo test`      | `dbx run -r test`                          |
| `turbo dev`       | `dbx run -r --parallel dev`                |
| `turbo.json`      | (optional) `run.tasks` in `vite.config.ts` |

Remove `turbo` and `turbo.json`. Ordering comes from each package's
`package.json` dependencies, so no `turbo.json` graph is needed.

## Per-workspace tasks

Each package declares `build`, `typecheck` and `test` in its own `vite.config.*`
(or `dbx.config.*`) with explicit cache input/output, so `dbx run` reports cache
hits (a `package.json` script cannot carry cache config). Use the Vite+ commands
rather than the individual tools:

```ts [packages/<pkg>/vite.config.ts]
import { defineConfig } from 'vite-plus';

export default defineConfig({
    run: {
        tasks: {
            build: {
                command: 'vp pack',
                cache: { input: [{ auto: true }, '!dist/**'], output: ['dist/**'] },
            },
            test: {
                command: 'vp test run',
                cache: { input: [{ auto: true }], output: [] },
            },
        },
    },
});
```

See the [Monorepo guide](/guide/monorepo) for the full task setup,
[Migrations](/guide/migrations/) for the `dbx migrate` reference, and
[Providers (Vite+)](/guide/providers) for the `dbx vite` passthrough.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/cli.md
---
# CLI

The `dbx` binary is composed from framework-agnostic command
descriptors. Commands that run against a project load its toolchain config —
the `dbx()` Vite plugin config when present, otherwise the nearest
`dbx.config.*` — so config-derived defaults apply unless you override them on the
command line.

## Global flags

| Flag                | Description                                                    |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--log-level <lvl>` | Minimum log level: `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`, `silent`. |
| `--color`           | Force coloured output (the default).                           |
| `--no-color`        | Disable coloured output (including help/error formatting).     |
| `--no-update-check` | Do not check for a newer `dbx` version.                        |
| `--config <file>`   | Use a specific config file instead of discovering one.         |
| `--no-config`       | Ignore config files and use CLI flags/env defaults only.       |
| `-H, --help`        | Display help for the program or subcommand.                    |
| `-V, --version`     | Output the version number.                                     |

These override the [`logger` config](/guide/config/logging) and may appear
before or after the subcommand. `--config` resolves relative to the current
directory (absolute paths are used as-is); `--no-config` skips discovery
entirely (including inherited parent configs).

`dbx` checks the npm registry in the background (about once a day) and prints a
short notice with a link to the release when a newer version is published. The
check is skipped in CI and when `NO_UPDATE_NOTIFIER` or `DBX_NO_UPDATE_CHECK` is
set, and can be turned off with `--no-update-check`.

## Interactive CLI

The CLI is scriptable first: every prompt has a flag equivalent. In a TTY,
however, some commands prompt when the flags are omitted:

```sh
dbx create                     # template + name + scope + template inputs/actions
dbx migrate --recursive        # choose the projects to migrate
```

`dbx migrate` detects migrations automatically without `--from`; the prompt is
only the project picker for `--recursive`. `--json`, a piped stdin, or the
explicit flags disable prompts. See [Scaffolding](#scaffolding) and
[Migrations](#migrations) for the flag forms.

## Output

Colour is on by default and follows `--no-color` / the [`logger` config](/guide/config/logging).
`--no-color` also disables the program's configured help/error colours (the
`dbx` program passes `disableColors` from the parsed global `color` flag).

## Core

| Command     | Description                                                                                                            |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `projects`  | Discover projects and write `.dbx/toolchain/projects.json`.                                                            |
| `sync`      | Regenerate every managed file (`--check`, `--recursive`, `--watch`, `--force`, `--only`, `--json`).                    |
| `watch`     | Sync once, then watch key inputs and re-sync.                                                                          |
| `reset`     | Remove generated files, the manifest and/or the config (`--all`, `--recursive`); reverts `tsconfig.overrides` first.   |
| `providers` | List registered providers + their commands (`--json`).                                                                 |
| `enable`    | Enable the toolchain (`--workspace` by default, or `--global`; `--json`).                                              |
| `disable`   | Disable the toolchain (`--workspace` by default, or `--global`; `--json`).                                             |
| `enabled`   | Print the resolved enabled state and scope (`--json`). A config `toolchain.enabled` wins over `.vscode/settings.json`. |

### Task-only sync

`dbx sync --only <tasks>` runs just the named sync tasks (comma-separated) and
does **not** prune files owned by the tasks it skipped. This is useful at the
end of a build, when only the tsconfig aliases/references need refreshing:

```sh
dbx sync --only tsconfig
```

Unknown task names fail with the list of available tasks.

## Scaffolding

| Command                  | Description                                                                                                      |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `project:init`           | A single-package TypeScript project (`--package-manager`).                                                       |
| `project:init:monorepo`  | A monorepo root (add `--example` for one example workspace).                                                     |
| `project:init:workspace` | A workspace package into an existing monorepo root.                                                              |
| `project:config`         | Generate `dbx.config.*` for projects missing one (TS/JS, `--skip-config` for graph only; folds `vite.config.*`). |
| `create`                 | Scaffold from a template (`--template`/`--kind`, `--name`, `--scope`, `--out`).                                  |

Templates that declare inputs/actions are prompted for them (`--var key=value`,
`--action <id>`), see [Templates](/guide/templates).

On an interactive terminal, a bare `dbx create` (no `--template`/`--kind`/`--name`)
prompts for the template, name and scope with clack; Ctrl-C cancels. See
[Templates](/guide/templates).

## Templates

| Command             | Description                                                                          |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `template:list`     | List templates (`--kind`, `--registry`, `--online`, `--json`).                       |
| `template:init`     | Write a `template.json` to a directory (`--kind`, `--name`, `--add`, `--no-global`). |
| `template:add`      | Record a source (auto-inits local; `--no-global` keeps it project-only).             |
| `template:remove`   | Remove a source by id or `type:locate`.                                              |
| `template:registry` | List/add/remove the global template search paths (`--vscode-dir`, `--clear`).        |
| `registry`          | List/add/remove/set template **or provider** registries (`--kind`, `--scope`).       |
| `template:info`     | Show one template.                                                                   |

See [Templates](/guide/templates).

## Migrations

```sh
dbx migrate --from biome --write           # .oxfmtrc.json + .oxlintrc.json
dbx migrate --from biome --from prettier --write  # several sources
dbx migrate --from biome --target vite --write
dbx migrate --from oxc --write             # .oxfmtrc/.oxlintrc -> dbx.config
dbx migrate --from all                     # every detected source
dbx migrate --from vite --recursive --write  # migrate every detected project
dbx migrate --recursive                    # interactive project picker
dbx migrate --check                        # CI: exit 1 when stale
dbx migrate:list
```

See [Migrations](/guide/migrations/).

## Tsconfig / cleanup / changelog / workflows

| Command                     | Description                                                                        |
| --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `tsconfig`                  | Regenerate workspace `tsconfig.json` files (`--restore [kind]` reverts overrides). |
| `cleanup` / `cleanup:turbo` | Remove build artifacts / the turbo cache.                                          |
| `changelog`                 | Derive the semver bump and update CHANGELOG + versions.                            |
| `workflow`                  | Trigger generated workflows with their vendor CLI (`gh`, `glab` or `az`).          |

### Workflows

`dbx workflow [id...]` runs every enabled workflow (or the named ids/custom ids/file
names) with the CLI for its provider:

```sh
dbx workflow                    # every enabled workflow
dbx workflow ci release         # by id
dbx workflow deploy.yml         # by file name
dbx workflow --list --json      # ids, paths and providers
dbx workflow ci --ref main      # pass a branch/ref
dbx workflow ci --gh /path/to/gh --glab glab --az az
```

GitHub uses `gh workflow run <file>`, GitLab `glab ci run` (the project's
configured CI file), and Azure `az pipelines run --name <pipeline>` (the file
stem by default). When the matching CLI is not installed the command reports it
and continues with the other workflows. See [CI](/guide/ci/) for the vendor
workflow config.

## Providers

Every provider subcommand is a passthrough. Vite+ commands are reachable both
directly and through the `vite` namespace:

```sh
dbx fmt                 # the active formatter (vp fmt when Oxc)
dbx run -r build        # forwards to `vp run -r build`
dbx vite dev            # explicit namespace (always works)
dbx vite:build          # named alias for `vp build`
```

A bare `dbx <command>` is forwarded to Vite+ when the name (or a Vite+ alias)
matches — built-in commands win, so `dbx migrate` stays the toolchain's
migration. The `vite` command forwards its operands verbatim, so **every** Vite+
CLI command and flag is reachable.

## Programmatic

The CLI is assembled from framework-agnostic command descriptors, so a consumer
can build its own program (or reuse the routing helpers):

```ts
import {
    createCli,
    runCli,
    builtinCommands,
    withCliContext,
    withDefaultVite,
    extractConfigSelection,
    extractLogOptions,
} from '@deltabox/toolchain/cli';
```

| Export                                 | Description                                                            |
| -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `createCli(commands?)`                 | Build the `dbx` engine program (global flags + built-in commands).     |
| `runCli(argv?)`                        | Parse and run the CLI (extracts logger flags, then defaults Vite+).    |
| `builtinCommands()`                    | The commands built into the root CLI (config commands need an engine). |
| `withCliContext(commands)`             | Wrap commands with dbx config loading, logging and framing.            |
| `withDefaultVite(argv, commandNames?)` | Insert `vite` before a bare Vite+ command (built-ins win).             |
| `extractLogOptions(argv)`              | Pull `--log-level` / `--color` / `--no-color` out of argv.             |
| `extractConfigSelection(argv)`         | Pull `--config <file>` / `--no-config` out of argv.                    |

`createCli(commands)` accepts a typed command array (for example from
`defineCliCommand`) and keeps the command/option types on `program.commands`;
`createCli()` uses `builtinCommands()`.

`extractLogOptions` makes the logger flags work before *or* after the
subcommand and stops at `--`, so a wrapped binary's own flags are never eaten.
`withDefaultVite` powers the bare-command passthrough described above:

```ts
extractLogOptions(['node', 'dbx', 'sync', '--no-color']);
// { argv: ['node', 'dbx', 'sync'], options: { color: false } }

withDefaultVite(['node', 'dbx', 'fmt', '--check']);
// ['node', 'dbx', 'vite', 'fmt', '--check']
```

## Config generator

The generic Zod/env config engine is not a `dbx` command: a consumer
builds an engine with `createConfigEngine` and registers the `config:*` commands
on its **own** CLI. See [Config Generator](/guide/config-generator/).

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/docker.md
---
# Docker

`@deltabox/toolchain-docker` generates a deployable, multi-stage `Dockerfile`, a
`.dockerignore` and a `docker-compose.yaml`. Containerization is **opt-in** and
happens only when you scaffold: the files are a starting point, not
`dbx sync`-managed artifacts, so you can edit them freely afterwards.

```sh
# Add Docker artifacts to a new project
dbx create --template express --name api --containerize

# Or scaffold with the project command
dbx project:init --name api --containerize
```

In VS Code, **Create from template...** asks *Containerize with Docker?*. The
setting `deltabox.toolchain.containerizeTemplates` supplies the default and is
used by the curated **Scaffold** flow. Programmatically, pass
`containerize: true` to `scaffoldTemplate()`.

Every scaffold gets `Dockerfile`, `.dockerignore` and `docker-compose.yaml` for
local development (`docker compose up --build`).

## Programmatic API

`dockerFiles()` renders the artifacts (without writing), and
`writeDockerFiles()` writes them to a project:

```ts
import { dockerFiles, writeDockerFiles } from '@deltabox/toolchain/docker';

const files = dockerFiles({
    cwd: process.cwd(),
    image: 'myapp/api',
    tag: 'latest',
    port: 3000,
});

const written = writeDockerFiles({
    cwd: process.cwd(),
    compose: true,
    force: true, // overwrite existing artifacts
});
```

| Option            | Default                     | What it does                                   |
| ----------------- | --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `image`           | project name                | OCI image name.                                |
| `tag`             | `latest`                    | Image tag.                                     |
| `port`            | `3000` / `8080`             | Port the runtime image exposes.                |
| `runtime`         | `auto`                      | `node`, `static`, `bun`, or detect.            |
| `entry`           | `dist/index.js`             | Built server entry for `node`/`bun` runtimes.  |
| `output`          | `dist`                      | Build output directory (`static` copies this). |
| `nodeVersion`     | `engines.node` or `22`      | Node.js version for non-Vite+ images.          |
| `baseImage`       | Vite+/Bun/Node image        | Override the build-stage image.                |
| `runtimeImage`    | Debian/Bun/nginx/Node image | Override the runtime image.                    |
| `user`            | `nobody` / `node` / `bun`   | Runtime user.                                  |
| `compose`         | `false`                     | Also render `docker-compose.yaml`.             |
| `healthcheck`     | `true`                      | Add an HTTP `HEALTHCHECK`.                     |
| `healthcheckPath` | `/`                         | Path the healthcheck requests.                 |
| `dockerfile`      | `Dockerfile`                | Dockerfile file name.                          |
| `dockerignore`    | `true`                      | Render `.dockerignore`.                        |

`writeDockerFiles()` does not overwrite existing files unless `force: true`
(scaffolding passes it for a fresh project). There is no `docker` config section
and no sync task: the generated files are yours to maintain.

## Images

* **Vite+ projects** build with
  `ghcr.io/voidzero-dev/vite-plus:latest`, install with `vp install`, build with
  `vp build`, and copy the resolved Node.js binary into the runtime stage.
* **Bun projects** use `oven/bun:1` to build and `oven/bun:1-slim` to run.
* **Other Node projects** use `node:<version>-bookworm-slim`.
* **Static sites** copy the build output into
  `nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:alpine`, so the container runs as a non-root
  user on port `8080`.

Server images run as a non-root user and get a `HEALTHCHECK` that requests
`http://127.0.0.1:<port><healthcheckPath>`.

## COPY sources and installs

The dependency-install stage copies only sources that exist when the Dockerfile
is generated: `package.json` plus the project's lockfile/workspace files
(`yarn.lock`/`.yarnrc.yml`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`/`pnpm-workspace.yaml`,
`package-lock.json`, `bun.lock`/`bun.lockb`). A Vite+ project also copies an
existing `.node-version` before `vp install`, so Vite+ selects the same Node.js
version in the image. No lockfile is assumed, and a missing lockfile is never
`COPY`ed, so a fresh scaffold builds.

The generated `.dockerignore` matches dependencies and build output at any
depth (`**/node_modules`, `**/dist`, the configured output directory, ...), so
nested workspace copies are excluded from the build context too.

Yarn Plug'n'Play projects do not get `node_modules`. Their runtime image copies
the generated `.pnp.cjs` (or `.pnp.js`), an optional `.pnp.loader.mjs`, and
`.yarn`, then starts Node with `--require ./.pnp.cjs` (and
`--experimental-loader` when the loader exists).

The declared package manager is the single source of truth: `packageManager` in
`package.json` (or the `packageManager` option) drives both the copied lockfiles
and the `RUN` command. A Bun-runtime project with no declared manager installs
with Bun; otherwise the declared manager wins, so `yarn.lock` is never paired
with `bun install`. When a Bun-runtime project declares yarn/pnpm/npm,
dependencies install in a `node:<version>` `deps` stage and the Bun image only
builds (the official Bun image has no npm/corepack). Without a lockfile the
install runs without a frozen flag (`yarn install`, `pnpm install`,
`npm install`, `bun install`, `vp install`).

## Detection

With `runtime: 'auto'` the generator reads `package.json`:

* a `vitepress build` script is a **static** site
  (`docs/.vitepress/dist`);
* a `bun build`/`bun ...` start script is a **Bun** server;
* a `start` script is a **Node** server;
* a `vp build` script without `start` is a **static** app;
* otherwise it falls back to a **Node** server.

url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/mcp.md
---
# MCP (Model Context Protocol)

`@deltabox/toolchain` ships an MCP server that exposes the dbx APIs to AI
harnesses and editors. It is a dependency-free stdio server, so it works with
any MCP client and does not pull the MCP SDK into your project.

```sh
dbx mcp:serve
```

The server exposes one tool per public dbx capability:

| Tool                 | Runs                                                         |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `dbx_sync`           | `dbx sync` (with `check`, `recursive`, `configless`, `only`) |
| `dbx_projects`       | `dbx projects`                                               |
| `dbx_providers`      | `dbx providers`                                              |
| `dbx_templates`      | `dbx template:list`                                          |
| `dbx_template_info`  | `dbx template:info`                                          |
| `dbx_changelog`      | `dbx changelog`                                              |
| `dbx_migrate`        | `dbx migrate` (preview unless `write`)                       |
| `dbx_project_config` | `dbx project:config`                                         |
| `dbx_tsconfig`       | `dbx tsconfig`                                               |
| `dbx_workflow`       | `dbx workflow`                                               |
| `dbx_run`            | an allowlisted `dbx` command                                 |

Every tool runs the project's own resolved `dbx` binary, so the MCP surface
always matches the CLI version the project pins. Plugin-mode projects work
without a `dbx.config.*` (the server reads the `dbx()` Vite plugin options).

## Install

```sh
dbx mcp:install --provider claude
dbx mcp:install --provider vscode --scope global
dbx mcp:install --provider custom --dir ./tools/mcp
```

`dbx mcp:list` prints the builtin providers and the exact files each one writes:

| Provider   | Project config       | Skill / instructions                            |
| ---------- | -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `claude`   | `.mcp.json`          | `.claude/skills/deltabox/SKILL.md`              |
| `codex`    | `.codex/config.toml` | `.codex/skills/deltabox/SKILL.md`               |
| `vscode`   | `.vscode/mcp.json`   | `.github/instructions/deltabox.instructions.md` |
| `opencode` | `opencode.json`      | `.opencode/skills/deltabox/SKILL.md`            |
| `pi`       | `.pi/mcp.json`       | `.pi/skills/deltabox/SKILL.md`                  |
| `custom`   | `<dir>/mcp.json`     | `<dir>/deltabox/SKILL.md`                       |

`--scope global` writes to the provider's user profile instead
(`~/.claude.json`, `~/.codex/config.toml`, `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`,
...). `--no-skills` writes only the MCP config, and `--json` prints the exact
paths that were written.

The VS Code extension exposes the same flow from **Install MCP server + skill...**
(and the Home view's Quick Actions).

url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/logger.md
---
# Logger

Every toolchain message goes through one logger, so output stays consistent and
respects a single configuration. The `logger` section controls its level,
colours and prefix.

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        logger: { level: 'debug', color: false, name: 'dbx' },
    },
});
```

## Options

| Option     | Type                                               | Default | Description                                            |
| ---------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `level`    | `debug` | `info` | `warn` | `error` | `silent` | `info`  | Minimum level to print.                                |
| `color`    | `boolean`                                          | `true`  | Force colours on/off.                                  |
| `name`     | `string`                                           | `dbx`   | Prefix for non-indented lines.                         |
| `suppress` | `string \| string[]`                               | none    | Silence warnings/errors by id, substring or `/regex/`. |
| `logger`   | `ToolchainLogger`                                  | none    | Custom logger implementation.                          |

Colour is **on by default** (the toolchain forces it rather than relying on TTY
autodetection); `--no-color` or `logger: { color: false }` turn it off. Human
output is rendered with [`@clack/prompts`](https://bombshell.dev/clack) — level
symbols (`•` info, `◆` success, `▲` warn, `■` error) and a guide.

## Custom logger

`logger.logger` accepts a `ToolchainLogger` (`raw`, `rawError`, `write`, `debug`,
`info`, `success`, `warn`, `error`). The toolchain still applies `level` and
`suppress` before delegating, so a custom sink receives only visible messages.

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
toolchain: {
    logger: {
        logger: {
            raw: m => process.stdout.write(`${m}\n`),
            rawError: m => process.stderr.write(`${m}\n`),
            write: () => {},
            debug: () => {},
            info: m => sink.info(m),
            success: m => sink.info(m),
            warn: m => sink.warn(m),
            error: m => sink.error(m),
        },
    },
}
```

## CLI overrides

| Flag                | Description                                                |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--log-level <lvl>` | Minimum level: `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`, `silent`. |
| `--color`           | Force coloured output (the default).                       |
| `--no-color`        | Disable coloured output.                                   |

They win over the config and may appear before or after the subcommand.
`--no-color` also disables the program's configured help/error colours.

## Machine output

`--json` (and provider passthroughs) write raw, unprefixed, undecorated output
through the same logger (`logger.raw`), so it is safe to pipe into `jq` or
another tool.

## Providers

Provider passthrough commands (Vite+) follow the logger's colour setting, and the
[`providers`](/guide/providers#colour) section can force provider colours on or
off independently. `color: false` runs the wrapped binary with `NO_COLOR=1` and
`FORCE_COLOR=0`.

## Programmatic API

```ts
import {
    configureLogger,
    createLogger,
    getLogger,
    isLogLevel,
    logger,
    normalizeLogLevel,
    setLogConfig,
    setLogOverrides,
} from '@deltabox/toolchain/shared';
```

| Export                             | Description                                            |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `logger`                           | The active logger (delegates to the current instance). |
| `createLogger(options?)`           | Build a logger with explicit options.                  |
| `setLogConfig(section)`            | Apply the `logger` config section.                     |
| `setLogOverrides(options)`         | Apply CLI overrides (win over the config).             |
| `configureLogger(options?)`        | Alias for `setLogOverrides`.                           |
| `isLogLevel` / `normalizeLogLevel` | Validate/coerce a level.                               |

Use `logger.info` for human messages and `logger.raw` for machine output; avoid
`console.log` so output stays consistent and respects the config and CLI flags.

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/watch.md
---
# Watch

The `watch` section configures `dbx watch`, which syncs once and then re-runs on
input changes.

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        watch: { enabled: true, debounce: 150 },
    },
});
```

## Options

| Option      | Type                 | Default              | Description                                 |
| ----------- | -------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `enabled`   | `boolean`            | enabled when defined | Watch by default.                           |
| `debounce`  | `number`             | `150`                | Debounce window in ms before a re-sync.     |
| `exclude`   | `string \| string[]` | common ignored paths | Glob(s) excluded from watching.             |
| `gitignore` | `boolean`            | `true`               | Respect `.gitignore` files (root + nested). |

`exclude` adds to the common ignored paths (`node_modules`, `.dbx`, `dist`,
`build`, ...), and `gitignore` also honours the repo's `.gitignore` files (root
and nested, each scoped to its own directory) so ignored directories are never
watched. Set `gitignore: false` to watch them anyway. The common list is
exported as `DEFAULT_IGNORE_PATTERNS` from `@deltabox/toolchain` and
`@deltabox/toolchain/shared` if you need to build on it.

```ts
watch: { exclude: ['**/fixtures/**'], gitignore: true }
```

## How it works

```sh
dbx watch
```

`dbx watch` runs one sync, then watches the config file plus every task's
`watch` globs and re-runs on change. A config change reloads the config (and
rebuilds the watched inputs) before re-syncing. Writes made by the sync itself
must not re-trigger a run, so a short quiet window follows each sync.

Only **input** files are watched (eg. `dbx.config.*`, `tsconfig.default.json`,
`tsconfig.workspaces.json`), never the generated outputs — so a sync can never
loop on its own writes.

Custom tsconfig names (`tsconfig.rootFile`, `tsconfig.defaultFile`) are watched
instead of the defaults. `dbx watch --list` prints the resolved inputs without
watching (`--json` adds the tsconfig file names; the VS Code extension reads it):

```sh
dbx watch --list --json
# { "globs": ["**/dbx.config.*", "tsconfig.workspaces.json", "**/tsconfig.default.json"],
#   "tsconfig": { "baseFile": "tsconfig.base.json", ... } }
```

`dbx watch --force` runs even when there is no `dbx.config.*`, and
`watch: false` / `watch: { enabled: false }` disables it (so a plain
`dbx watch` warns and exits).

## VS Code

The VS Code extension has its own debounced scheduler that mirrors this
behaviour (see [VS Code Extension](/guide/vscode#auto-sync)); the `watch` section
configures the **CLI** `dbx watch` command.

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/changelog.md
---
# Changelog

## CI

The `ci` section drives everything Conventional Commits (by default): the CI that lints
commit messages, the local commit hook, the `commitlint.config.mjs`, the GitHub
workflows, and the changelog pipeline that bumps versions and writes
`CHANGELOG.md`. Its `ci.changelog` config holds the changelog-specific options.

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        ci: {
            ci: true,
            release: true,
            changelog: {
                branches: { main: 'main', dev: 'dev' },
                commitlint: {
                    types: ['feat', 'fix', 'docs', 'chore'],
                    scopes: ['api', 'web', 'deps'],
                },
                versioning: { target: 'individual', workspaces: ['packages/*', 'apps/*'] },
            },
        },
    },
});
```

`dbx sync` writes the opted-in GitHub workflows (`.github/workflows`), the
commitlint config, and the `commit-msg` hook. On a Vite+ project the hook is
`.vite-hooks/commit-msg`, installed by `vp hooks enable` / `vp config`; projects
without Vite+ keep the husky fallback (`.husky/commit-msg`). Activate the
dispatcher with a `postinstall` script:

```json [package.json]
{
    "scripts": {
        "commitlint": "commitlint",
        "postinstall": "vp hooks enable"
    }
}
```

For Vite+ projects, add a `.vite-hooks/pre-commit` running `vp staged` and put
the staged checks in the root `vite.config.ts` (`staged: { '*': 'vp check --fix' }`). See [Package scripts](/guide/scripts) for the full recommended script
set.

## Group order and titles

`groups` customizes the Conventional-Commits sections. It works on both
`toolchain.changelog.groups` (manual runs) and `ci.changelog.groups` (CI + manual
when inherited). An array sets the order and optionally the titles:

```ts
ci: {
    changelog: {
        groups: [
            { type: 'feat', title: 'New Features' },
            { type: 'fix', title: 'Bug Fixes' },
            'perf',
        ],
    },
}
```

A record is a shorthand for the same thing, ordered by its keys. Use `false` to
hide a group:

```ts
groups: {
    feat: 'New Features',
    fix: 'Bug Fixes',
    chore: false,
}
```

The default order is **Breaking Changes**, `feat`, `fix`, then the remaining
types (`perf`, `refactor`, `docs`, ...). Types you do not mention are appended in
the default order. `order` overrides the array/record position, and every
title/order/hidden value accepts a callback. The whole `groups` value can also be
a callback, so it can be computed from the types/items in the current run:

```ts
groups: context => [
    {
        type: 'feat',
        title: group => `New Features (${group.groupItems.length})`,
        order: 0,
    },
    { type: 'fix', hidden: group => group.groupItems.length === 0 },
    ...context.types.filter(type => !['feat', 'fix'].includes(type)),
];
```

Callbacks are TS/JS-config-only. `dbx changelog --format-only` also uses the
configured order/titles when regrouping existing entries.

`groups` only groups **commit sections** inside one version. To treat several
changelog versions as one release body, use
[`release.group`](/guide/ci/releases#grouped-release-bodies) instead.

## Breaking-change detection

Breaking commits are detected by Conventional Commits rules by default: a `!`
before the subject colon (`feat!:`, `feat(scope)!:`) or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` /
`BREAKING-CHANGE:` footer line. Configure `breaking` on either
`toolchain.changelog` or `ci.changelog` to override it:

```ts
breaking: 'conventional', // default
// breaking: 'any',       // legacy loose match anywhere in the subject/body
// breaking: false,       // disable breaking detection
// breaking: { pattern: '^feat!:' },
// breaking: { match: 'BREAKING CHANGE' },
// breaking: ({ subject, body }) => subject.includes('!'),
```

The same setting is used for version bumps, changelog grouping and
`--format-only` regrouping.

## Manual `toolchain.changelog`

The top-level `changelog` section configures manual runs for `dbx changelog`, the
VS Code actions and the programmatic API. It accepts the pipeline options
(commitlint, versioning, groups, VS Code settings), but not the CI-only workflow
options or `branches`:

```ts [manual pipeline]
toolchain: {
    changelog: {
        commitlint: { types: ['feat'], scopes: ['api'] },
        versioning: true,
        vscode: true,
    },
}
```

Move the generated workflows to the top-level `ci` section, and put the pipeline
options under `ci.changelog` when CI should use them too. Branches and workflow
overrides only exist on `ci.changelog`:

```ts [after]
toolchain: {
    ci: {
        ci: true,
        release: true,
        changelog: {
            branches: { main: 'main' },
            commitlint: { types: ['feat'], scopes: ['api'] },
            versioning: true,
            vscode: true,
        },
    },
}
```

`ci.changelog` inherits `toolchain.changelog` when it is enabled without
pipeline options (`ci.changelog: true`, a raw workflow string, or workflow-only
overrides). Options set explicitly on `ci.changelog` win.

## GitHub metadata

When `gh` is installed and authenticated, a run resolves commit authors, PR
credit and issue titles/links from GitHub. Lookups are batched so a large range
stays close to a handful of requests:

* one REST `compare/{base}...{head}` request per scanned range for commit
  authors;
* GraphQL `associatedPullRequests` lookups in batches of 100 commits (a PR
  author wins over the commit author, matching the changelog credit rules);
* aliased GraphQL issue lookups, 100 issues per request.

Without `gh` (or with `DBX_NO_GH=1`) the pipeline falls back to git metadata and
plain `#123` references. Commits that no remote-tracking ref reaches are skipped
(GitHub cannot resolve an unpushed SHA), and terminal client errors (eg. a 404
for a missing ref) are not retried. Other failures are retried
`DBX_GH_MAX_RETRIES` times (default 5) with a `DBX_GH_RETRY_DELAY` ms delay
(default 3000), then `gh` is disabled for the rest of the run. Set `DBX_GH_BIN`
to point at a different `gh` executable.

## Where to start

* [CI](/guide/ci/) — the opt-in GitHub workflows (CI checks, changelog, release,
  issues, sync) and their common settings.
* [Branches](/guide/changelog/branches) — `main`/`dev` branch globs.
* [commitlint](/guide/changelog/commitlint) — config location, types/scopes and
  the no-commitlint fallback.
* [Versioning](/guide/changelog/versioning) — which `package.json` versions a run
  bumps.
* [CLI](/guide/changelog/cli) — running the changelog locally.
* [Writing commit messages](/guide/changelog/writing-commit-messages) — avoiding
  shell-mangled messages.
* [Troubleshooting](/guide/changelog/troubleshooting) — the upstream commitlint
  parser-preset error.
* [Releases](/guide/ci/releases) — the aggregated release PR body.

url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/changelog/branches.md

# Branches

`ci.changelog.branches.main` and `ci.changelog.branches.dev` pick which branches
the generated workflows target. Each accepts a glob or an array of globs:

| Branch | Drives                                                                         | Default              |
| ------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------- |
| `main` | The **CI** workflow (push), the **release** workflow, and the release PR base. | `['main']`           |
| `dev`  | The **changelog/version** workflow (push).                                     | none — reuses `main` |

`dev` has **no default**: when it is omitted the changelog workflow runs on
`main` (so a single-branch repo needs no `dev`). Set it for a `dev` → `main`
flow:

```ts
ci: { changelog: { branches: { main: 'main', dev: 'dev' } } }
// or multiple branches per purpose:
ci: { changelog: { branches: { main: ['main', 'release/**'], dev: ['dev', 'next'] } } }
```

The `sync` workflow runs on both. Any per-workflow `pushBranches` override (eg.
`ci.release.pushBranches`) still wins.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/changelog/cli.md
---
# CLI

```sh
dbx changelog                       # bump + write (uses ci.changelog.versioning)
dbx changelog --dry-run             # preview the root entry
dbx changelog --range v1.2.0..HEAD  # scan a specific range
dbx changelog --version 2.0.0       # force a version (retags the changelogs)
dbx changelog --format-only         # regroup existing changelogs, no bump
dbx changelog --release-body 2.0.0 # print the release PR body for a version
dbx changelog --release-body 2.0.0 --release-group          # group since the last release
dbx changelog --release-body 2.0.0 --release-since v1.9.0   # explicit boundary
dbx changelog --release-body 2.0.0 --no-release-group       # disable configured grouping
```

The command reads `ci.changelog` and falls back to the manual
`toolchain.changelog` pipeline options (commitlint, versioning, vscode). This
lets a project keep manual/API changelog runs without enabling the CI workflow;
`ci.changelog` inherits the same options when it does not override them.

The generated `changelog` workflow runs `dbx changelog --range ...` on every push
to the `dev` branches (or `main` when `dev` is unset), so versioning is applied
from CI as well as locally.

`dbx workflow [id...]` triggers the generated workflows with their vendor CLI
(`gh`, `glab` or `az`); with no ids it triggers every workflow you declared under
`toolchain.ci`. See [Workflows](/guide/cli#workflows).

## Formatting

`--format-only` regroups the existing entries without bumping versions. It keeps
list items, unwraps hard-wrapped lines, keeps multi-line `BREAKING CHANGE:`
footers together and preserves fenced code blocks. Numeric-only short hashes
(eg. `#4033009`) are resolved against git, so they stay commit links while real
issue numbers stay issue links. Existing subjects and descriptions are never
re-rendered from git: hand corrections (including backtick fixes) survive, and a
description is only filled in when the entry has none. See
[Writing commit messages](/guide/changelog/writing-commit-messages).

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/changelog/commitlint.md
---
# commitlint

By default the generated `commitlint.config.mjs` lives at the project root. Set
`ci.changelog.commitlint.dir` to write it elsewhere:

```ts
ci: {
    changelog: {
        commitlint: {
            dir: '.config';
        }
    }
} // -> .config/commitlint.config.mjs
```

When a custom dir is set, the generated commit hook and the CI commitlint step
both pass `--config <dir>/commitlint.config.mjs`, so commitlint finds it. Note
that editor tooling that discovers the config by convention (eg. the
Conventional Commits VS Code extension, which loads from the repo root) expects
the config at the root — keep the default unless you have a reason to move it.

`commitlint.types` and `commitlint.scopes` are the allowed Conventional-Commits
types/scopes:

```ts
ci: {
    changelog: {
        commitlint: {
            types: ['feat', 'fix', 'docs', 'chore'],
            scopes: ['api', 'web', 'deps'],
        },
    },
}
```

## Disabling commitlint

Set `ci.changelog.commitlint: false` (or `{ enabled: false }`) to generate
changelogs **without** the Conventional-Commits rules. The changelog workflow is
still generated, but dbx writes no `commitlint.config.mjs`, no commit hook and no
commitlint step in the CI workflow.

The changelog then falls back to a coarse grouping: commits are hoisted into
`Major changes`, `Minor changes` and `Patch changes` buckets (breaking commits
and `feat:` go to major/minor; everything else is a patch), while the package
changes section (eg. new packages) is kept. This is intentionally less detailed
than the rule/scope grouping, but it works with any commit-message style.

> The extension's `No "exports" main defined in ... conventional-changelog-conventionalcommits ...`
> error is an upstream commitlint bug (ESM-only parser preset), not a config
> discovery problem. See [Troubleshooting](/guide/changelog/troubleshooting).

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/changelog/intro-outro.md
---
# Intro and outro text

`toolchain.changelog.intro` and `toolchain.changelog.outro` add custom text to the
newest changelog entry. They are opt-in: when the section is absent or an entry
is disabled, nothing is added. `ci.changelog` inherits the same options.

Each setting accepts one entry or an array (`Arrayable`). An entry contains:

| Field     | Description                                                                                                    |
| --------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `content` | The text to insert. Mutually exclusive with `file`.                                                            |
| `file`    | A file whose contents are inserted (relative to the repo root or absolute). Mutually exclusive with `content`. |
| `target`  | A workspace path relative to the repo root, `.` for the root, or a glob like `apps/*`.                         |
| `include` | Only apply to workspaces whose repo-relative directory matches these globs (tsconfig-style include).           |
| `exclude` | Skip workspaces whose repo-relative directory matches these globs.                                             |
| `enabled` | Set `false` to skip the entry (default `true`).                                                                |

Intro text is placed before the version body; outro text is appended after it.
Entries are applied in config order, and multiple matching entries are joined
with a blank line. Workspaces outside `ci.changelog.versioning.workspaces` (or
the default workspace fallback) are skipped.

```ts
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        changelog: {
            intro: [
                { target: '.', content: '> **Pre-release:** APIs may change.' },
                { include: 'apps/*', file: 'docs/CHANGELOG.intro.md' },
            ],
            outro: {
                target: 'packages/ui',
                content: '_Thanks to everyone who contributed!_',
            },
        },
    },
});
```

The same target selector is reused by the scoped versioning options
(`prerelease`, `bump`, `allowOverBump`, `commit`, `provider`); see
[Versioning](/guide/changelog/versioning#targeted-options).

### CLI flags

You can add an intro/outro without editing the config:

`sh
dbx changelog --intro "> **Beta:** APIs may change." --outro-file CHANGELOG.outro.md
dbx changelog --intro-file CHANGELOG.intro.md --outro "Thanks to all contributors!"
`

Flags are appended to the configured entries (config is still loaded from the
dbx() Vite plugin or dbx.config.\*). The intro is rendered below the version
heading.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/changelog/troubleshooting.md
---
# Troubleshooting

## `No "exports" main defined in ... conventional-changelog-conventionalcommits`

Seen from the Conventional Commits VS Code extension (`vivaxy.vscode-conventional-commits`),
usually alongside empty type/scope suggestions and a `The cwd is ...` line:

```
commitlint: Error: No "exports" main defined in
  node_modules/conventional-changelog-conventionalcommits/package.json
```

This is a **known upstream commitlint bug** (commitlint#4864): the generated
config `extends: ['@commitlint/config-conventional']`, which sets
`parserPreset: 'conventional-changelog-conventionalcommits'`, and v10 of that
package is **ESM-only** (`exports` has no `require`/`default`), so the extension's
bundled (older) commitlint cannot `require.resolve` it. The config is read fine —
the *preset* fails to resolve, so the extension falls back to empty rules.

The commit hook and CI are unaffected when commitlint is recent enough to resolve
pure-ESM presets (commitlint ≥ 21.2.3). If your local commitlint is older, pin
the preset to the last CJS-compatible release:

```json [package.json]
{
    "resolutions": { "conventional-changelog-conventionalcommits": "9.3.1" }
}
```

(Use `overrides` instead of `resolutions` for npm.) Updating the extension to a
version bundling the fixed commitlint also resolves it.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/changelog/versioning.md
---
# Versioning

`ci.changelog.versioning` controls whether — and where — a changelog run writes
`version` fields into `package.json`. It accepts a boolean or an object, and
defaults to `true`.

```ts
ci: { changelog: { versioning: true } }                       // uniform, defaults
ci: { changelog: { versioning: false } }                      // never write versions
ci: { changelog: { versioning: { target: 'root-only' } } }
ci: { changelog: { versioning: { target: 'individual', workspaces: ['packages/*'] } } }
```

## `target`

| Target       | What it bumps                                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `uniform`    | The root (when it has a `package.json`) **and every workspace** to one shared version. **Default.**                                                                          |
| `root-only`  | Only the root `package.json`. Workspaces are left untouched and get no changelog entry.                                                                                      |
| `individual` | The root tracks the overall bump; **each workspace is bumped on its own** from the commits touching its files, so versions can drift apart (like an "independent" monorepo). |

With `versioning: false` no `version` field is written at all — the changelog
entries are still generated (headed as `uniform` would), so you can keep
versioning in another tool (for example changesets).

## `workspaces`

An array of glob patterns selecting the workspaces to version, relative to the
repo root. It resolves in this order:

1. the `workspaces` patterns you pass, when you pass them;
2. otherwise the root `package.json` `workspaces` field, when present;
3. otherwise the root `package.json` alone (a single-package repo);
4. otherwise a warning is logged and nothing is versioned.

```ts
ci: {
    changelog: {
        versioning: {
            target: 'individual',
            workspaces: ['packages/*', '!packages/private-*'],
        },
    },
}
```

Glob negation (`!pattern`) is honoured: the excluded workspaces are removed from
the set, so private packages are never versioned or given a changelog.

`individual` uses a `git log` path filter per workspace, so a workspace is only
bumped when the scanned commit range touched a file inside it — or a file in one
of the workspaces it depends on (see [Workspace changelogs](#workspace-changelogs)).
The root's version always follows the overall bump derived from every scanned
commit.

Re-runs are idempotent: commits already listed in a workspace's own `CHANGELOG.md`
are filtered out before the bump is derived. A workspace with no new commits is
skipped entirely (no bump, no duplicate entry), and an old `feat` cannot re-bump a
workspace as a minor on a later run.

## `prerelease`

Set a tag such as `beta` or `rc` to keep a release on a prerelease channel:

```ts
ci: { changelog: { versioning: { target: 'individual', prerelease: 'beta' } } }
```

* A stable version bumps its core and starts the channel:
  `1.0.0` + a minor bump → `1.1.0-beta.0`.
* An existing prerelease keeps its core and increments the counter instead of
  bumping again: `1.1.0-beta.0` → `1.1.0-beta.1`.
* Switching tags keeps the core and starts the new channel at `.0`:
  `1.1.0-alpha.2` → `1.1.0-beta.0`.
* The suffix is checked before it is applied, so it is never appended twice.

The tag is a single identifier (`^[0-9A-Za-z-]+$`); the numeric counter is added
automatically. The same rule applies to `uniform`, `root-only` and `individual`
targets, including each workspace's own version in `individual` mode.

A stable release can group every prerelease since the last stable release into
one GitHub Release body with `changelog.release.group: true`. See
[Grouped release bodies](/guide/ci/releases#grouped-release-bodies).

## Version hooks

Use [`toolchain.hooks.beforeVersion`](/guide/config/hooks#beforeversion) for
work that must happen before the writes (for example a release guard), and
[`toolchain.hooks.afterVersion`](/guide/config/hooks#afterversion) for work that
must follow a version bump, such as syncing a scaffold catalog:

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
hooks: {
    beforeVersion: ({ previousVersion, version }) => {
        assertReleaseAllowed(previousVersion, version);
    },
    afterVersion: ({ cwd }) => syncScaffoldCatalog(cwd),
},
```

Both hooks receive the repository root and the new version (`beforeVersion`
also receives `previousVersion`); async hooks are awaited. The generated
changelog workflow stages `.yarnrc.yml` with the bump, so a catalog update lands
in the same commit.

## How a run decides its versions

Each run:

1. reads the commits in the range (`--range`/`--processing-method`, default
   `HEAD`);
2. derives the semver bump (`feat` → minor, `fix`/other → patch, `!` or a
   `BREAKING CHANGE` footer → major);
3. plans the versions per `target` + `workspaces` (see above);
4. writes the plan's `package.json` versions and prepends the new entry to the
   root `CHANGELOG.md` and each versioned workspace's `CHANGELOG.md`.

Use `dbx changelog --dry-run` to preview the proposed root entry without touching
any file; the log line reports the active `target` (or `disabled`).

## Workspace changelogs

Each versioned workspace gets **its own `CHANGELOG.md`** (created if missing),
headed by the version the plan assigned it. A workspace's entry only lists its
**related commits**: those touching the workspace directory **or any workspace it
transitively depends on**, resolved from the project dependency graph
(`.dbx/toolchain/projects.json`, written by `dbx projects`). So a change in a
shared package shows up in the changelog of every package that consumes it, not
just in its own.

Without a graph (eg. `dbx projects` was never run), a workspace falls back to
filtering on its own directory only. A workspace with no related commits is
skipped (no empty entry, no file created).

## Package changes footer

By default the root entry ends with a `### Package changes` footer comparing the
working tree against the previous released version. It reads dependency fields
from every `package.json` and the package-manager catalogs:

* Yarn: `.yarnrc.yml` (`catalog:` and named `catalogs:`);
* pnpm: `pnpm-workspace.yaml` (`catalog:` and named `catalogs:`);
* Bun: `package.json` `workspaces.catalog` / `catalogs`.

Catalog entries are diffed in the same map as declared dependencies, so a
catalog-only range change is reported under the root package at both ends of the
release. Entries are grouped by the declaring package (one top-level bullet per
package, with each changed dependency nested under it). Pass
`--no-package-changes-section` to omit the footer.

`--format-only` recomputes each released entry's footer from its release refs.
The newest entry is usually unreleased, so its footer compares the working tree
with the previous release — the same diff `dbx changelog` wrote. A tagged newest
entry keeps its ref-to-ref diff and never picks up uncommitted dependency
changes.

## Custom bump rules

`versioning.bump` maps `major`, `minor` and `patch` to a matcher.
Matchers can be booleans, substrings, `/regex/` strings, arrays, objects
(`{ type, types, scope, scopes, pattern, match, breaking }`) or callbacks.

```ts
ci: {
    changelog: {
        versioning: {
            bump: {
                major: { scope: 'api', breaking: true },
                minor: [{ type: 'feat' }, /^feat\(ui\)/],
                patch: 'fix',
            },
            // Apply one bump per matching change instead of once per run.
            allowOverBump: false,
        },
    },
}
```

Callbacks receive `{ env, logger, packageJson?, commit }` and may return a
boolean or a version index.

## Commit credits and formatting

`versioning.commit` controls the commit bullet credits. All options default to
`true` except `authorAvatar`.

```ts
ci: {
    changelog: {
        versioning: {
            commit: {
                author: true,
                authorAvatar: true,
                commitSha: true,
                issues: true,
                format: ({ commit, author, issues, repo }) =>
                    `${commit.subject} — ${author.name}${issues.length ? ` (${issues.length} issues)` : ''}`,
            },
        },
    },
}
```

## Providers

`versioning.provider` selects the changelog provider:

* `default` (or omitted) uses the built-in pipeline.
* `changesets` runs `npx changeset version` and leaves changelog/version output
  to changesets.
* a callback `(ctx) => string | void` can replace the summary.
* an object `{ id, run(ctx) }` can run custom logic and optionally return the
  summary string.

## Targeted options

prerelease, `bump.{major,minor,patch}`, `allowOverBump`, `commit` and
`provider` accept either the plain value or a scoped form:

`ts
ci: {
    changelog: {
        versioning: {
            prerelease: [
                { target: 'packages/ui', options: 'beta' },
                { include: 'apps/*', options: 'rc' },
            ],
            bump: { minor: [{ target: 'packages/core', options: /^feat/ }] },
            allowOverBump: [{ target: 'packages/ui', options: true }],
            commit: [{ exclude: 'packages/legacy', options: { authorAvatar: true } }],
            provider: [{ target: '.', options: { id: 'custom', run: ctx => ctx.records.length + ' commits' } }],
        },
    },
}
`

Each scoped entry shares the same selector as `toolchain.changelog.intro` /
`outro`: `target` (a workspace path, `.` for the root, or a glob like
`apps/*`), `include` and `exclude`. The narrowest matching target wins; when
nothing matches, the plain value is used. Workspaces outside
`versioning.workspaces` are never considered.

`Arrayable` entries (one value or an array) are supported for every targeted
option and for the intro/outro settings.

## Collapsible details

`versioning.commit.details` wraps changelog sections in markdown
`<details>`/`<summary>` blocks. It is enabled by default; `details: false` opts
out.

* `descriptions` (default on) nests a commit's description body under its bullet
  as a collapsible whose summary is `**See more...**`.
* `breaking` (default on) wraps the breaking section; the summary names the
  section, so the duplicate heading is not repeated inside.
* The version stays a normal `##` heading. `--release-body-wrap` wraps the body
  with the `**Release notes**` summary and `details.body` is opt-out there; in
  non-wrapping mode `details.body` is opt-in.
* `intro`/`outro`/`footer` are opt-in wrappers; `types` (default on) wraps the
  CC type sections, leaving the generated `Package changes`/`New contributors`
  footers alone.

Summaries accept inline Markdown, which is converted to HTML (`<strong>`,
`<em>`, `<code>`, links, images and `<del>`) because Markdown is not parsed
inside `<summary>`. Heading elements are not used there; summaries are bold or
plain inline content.

```ts
ci: {
    changelog: {
        versioning: {
            commit: {
                details: {
                    descriptions: { title: 'More', expanded: true },
                    releaseNotes: { title: 'Release notes' },
                    intro: true,
                    outro: true,
                    footer: true,
                    breaking: false,
                    types: ['feat', 'fix'],
                    custom: { start: '<!-- details:start -->', end: '<!-- details:end -->' },
                },
            },
        },
    },
}
```

* `descriptions` uses `See more...` by default and only applies when the commit has a body; the collapsible is nested under the commit bullet.
* `releaseNotes`/`body` use `Release notes` by default; `breaking`/`types` use the section title (bold for breaking).
* `intro`, `outro` and `footer` keep inline summaries.
* `types` (default on) wraps CC type sections (all types when `true`), using the section title by default.
* `minCommits` on a toggle skips the collapsible until that section has at least
  N commit entries. A top-level `minCommits` sets the default for every section;
  a nested value wins. The body defaults to **10** commits.
* `custom` accepts a regex/string or `{ start, end }` markers; the match (or start match) becomes the summary.

Every flag also accepts `{ title?: string; expanded?: boolean }`.

### Details lifecycle

`details.lifecycle` controls when wrapping happens:

* `after` (default): details are applied to the fully formatted entry. Custom
  `RegExp`/string searches therefore match the formatted text (bold headings,
  credits, etc.).
* `before`: details are applied while the entry is rendered.

`details.body` wraps the whole version body in a collapsible titled
`Release notes`. It is opt-in normally and opt-out with
`--release-body-wrap`, and requires at least 10 commits (`minCommits`) when
enabled unless overridden. Release body wrapping uses `details.releaseNotes`
with the same title by default.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/changelog/writing-commit-messages.md
---
# Writing commit messages

The changelog is rendered from commit **subjects and bodies**, so what you commit
is what readers see. Watch out for characters that a **shell** re-interprets —
especially when a message is drafted by an **AI/LLM** and committed through
`git commit -m "..."`.

## Shell escaping

* **PowerShell** treats a backtick as its escape character, so `` `r `` / `` `n `` /
  `` `t `` / `` `b `` become CR / LF / TAB / backspace. A preceding `\` is left
  behind, so `` `resolveVite `` can land in the changelog as a stray `\`, a CR and
  `esolveVite`.
* **bash** runs an unquoted `` `...` `` as command substitution, and `$(...)` / `${...}`
  expand before `git` ever sees them.

The result is invisible control characters, stray `\` and dropped letters.
`sanitizeText` maps the common control characters back to the letter they
replaced (`BEL`→`a`, `BS`→`b`, `FF`→`f`, `VT`→`v`, `TAB`→`t`, `LF`→`n`,
`CR`→`r`, `ESC`→`e`, `NUL`→`0`) and drops the stray `\`, so words like `any`,
`false` and `bin` are restored. It also repairs the common backtick-to-backslash
artifacts (a paired `\yarn cache dir\` or a lone trailing `baseTsdownConfig\`)
back to inline code, while leaving Windows paths and regexes alone. A character
the shell consumed without leaving a trace still cannot be recovered.

## Authoring safely

* Prefer a **file over `-m`**: `git commit -F message.txt`, or a quoted heredoc
  (`git commit -F - <<'EOF' ... EOF`) — nothing is re-interpreted. Avoid assembling
