  multi-line messages inline in PowerShell.
* When an AI/LLM drafts the message, strip **typographic characters** before
  committing: curly quotes (`’ “ ”`), em/en dashes (`— –`), non-breaking spaces,
  zero-width characters and emoji all survive into the changelog and can break
  `commitlint` or the markdown.
* **Preview the entry**: `dbx changelog --dry-run` prints the proposed entry —
  check it for stray `\`, `\r`, `\b`, `\t` or mojibake before releasing.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/ci.md
---
# CI

`dbx sync` writes the opted-in workflows for **GitHub Actions**, **GitLab CI**
and **Azure Pipelines**. Every workflow is **opt-in**: declare it under
`toolchain.ci` to write it; omit it (or set it to `false`) and the toolchain
leaves that file unmanaged. Every workflow id (`ci`, `changelog`, `release`,
`issues`, `sync`) accepts one of four forms:

* `true` / `false` — write the generated GitHub default, or skip it;
* a **`WorkflowOptions` object** — override parts of the GitHub default
  (branches, triggers, extra top-level keys, extra steps/jobs, token overrides);
* a **complete vendor workflow** — `{ provider, workflow }` for `github`,
  `gitlab` or `azure`, written as-is;
* a **raw YAML string** — written **verbatim** as the workflow file, for a
  workflow the object model can't express.

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        ci: {
            ci: true, // the generated GitHub CI checks
            issues: false, // don't write issues.yml
            release: { pushBranches: ['main'] }, // override the GitHub default
            changelog: { branches: { main: 'main', dev: 'dev' } },
            // A complete GitLab pipeline, written to `.gitlab-ci.yml`:
            sync: {
                provider: 'gitlab',
                workflow: {
                    stages: ['check'],
                    check: { stage: 'check', script: ['yarn dbx sync --check'] },
                },
            },
        },
    },
});
```

A raw string is **not** merged with the default, is **not** token-replaced, and
gets **no generated header** — it is the file's exact content. The
`ci.changelog.branches` defaults don't apply to it either (it defines its own
triggers). An empty string disables the workflow.

The `ci` key doubles as the CI-checks workflow (`ci.yml`) and the section name, so
`toolchain.ci.ci` is the checks workflow. Set `toolchain.ci.enabled` to `false` to
disable the whole section (and every nested workflow) at once.

## Vendor workflows

A complete vendor workflow always has `provider` and `workflow`; `filename`,
`dir` and `enabled` are optional:

| `provider` | Default file          | Run with           |
| ---------- | --------------------- | ------------------ |
| `github`   | `.github/workflows/`  | `gh workflow run`  |
| `gitlab`   | `.gitlab-ci.yml`      | `glab ci run`      |
| `azure`    | `azure-pipelines.yml` | `az pipelines run` |

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
toolchain: {
    ci: {
        // .gitlab-ci.yml (the default GitLab path)
        ci: {
            provider: 'gitlab',
            workflow: { stages: ['test'], test: { stage: 'test', script: ['yarn test'] } },
        },
        // azure-pipelines.yml (the default Azure path)
        release: {
            provider: 'azure',
            workflow: { trigger: ['main'], pool: { vmImage: 'ubuntu-latest' }, steps: [] },
        },
        // A complete GitHub workflow, written to the default `.github/workflows/deploy.yml`
        custom: {
            deploy: {
                provider: 'github',
                workflow: {
                    name: 'Deploy',
                    on: { push: { branches: ['main'] } },
                    jobs: { deploy: { 'runs-on': 'ubuntu-latest', steps: [] } },
                },
            },
        },
    },
}
```

`filename` and `dir` override the generated path for any provider. The workflow
object is written as-is (only the toolchain's {{ token }} replacements are
applied), so it must be a complete pipeline. `dbx workflow` dispatches each
workflow with its vendor CLI — see [CLI](/guide/cli#tsconfig-cleanup-changelog-workflows).

## Typed GitHub workflows

If you prefer a typed builder over hand-writing YAML, use
[`@github-actions-workflow-ts/lib`](https://github.com/emmanuelnk/github-actions-workflow-ts)
(and its `@github-actions-workflow-ts/actions` catalog). The builder produces a
plain workflow object in `.workflow`, which the `github` vendor form accepts:

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
import { ActionsCheckoutV4, ActionsSetupNodeV4 } from '@github-actions-workflow-ts/actions';
import { NormalJob, Step, Workflow } from '@github-actions-workflow-ts/lib';

import { defineConfig, type GitHubWorkflow } from '@deltabox/toolchain';

const test = new NormalJob('test', { 'runs-on': 'ubuntu-latest' });
test.addStep(new ActionsCheckoutV4({ name: 'Checkout' }));
test.addStep(new ActionsSetupNodeV4({ name: 'Setup Node', with: { 'node-version': '22' } }));
test.addStep(new Step({ name: 'Test', run: 'yarn test' }));

const ci = new Workflow('ci.yml', {
    name: 'CI',
    on: { push: { branches: ['main'] } },
});
ci.addJob(test);

export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        ci: {
            ci: {
                provider: 'github',
                workflow: ci.workflow as unknown as GitHubWorkflow,
            },
        },
    },
});
```

The toolchain does not depend on the builder, so the `workflow` field is typed
from its own vendored GitHub schema. The two schemas can drift slightly (for
example the builder's `Partial<Workflow>` makes `on` optional, and its
`permissions` allows `id-token: read`), so cast the object when TypeScript
rejects it. At runtime the workflow is validated by GitHub, exactly like a
hand-written object.

## Workflows

| Workflow   | GitHub file      | Page                                      |
| ---------- | ---------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| CI checks  | `ci.yml`         | [CI checks](/guide/ci/ci)                 |
| Changelog  | `changelog.yml`  | [Changelog workflow](/guide/ci/changelog) |
| Release    | `release.yml`    | [Releases](/guide/ci/releases)            |
| Issues     | `issues.yml`     | [Issues](/guide/ci/issues)                |
| Toolchain  | `sync.yml`       | [Sync](/guide/ci/sync)                    |
| Dependabot | `dependabot.yml` | [Dependabot](/guide/ci/dependabot)        |

`ci.dependabot.security` additionally writes
`.github/workflows/dependabot-security.yml` to enable GitHub's native security
updates and apply a severity threshold.

Extra workflows can be defined under `toolchain.ci.custom.<id>` (for example
`ci.custom.deploy` writes `.github/workflows/deploy.yml`, or the vendor default
when it sets `provider`). Each accepts the same workflow forms, plus `filename`
and `dir` overrides.

See [Workflow settings](/guide/ci/settings) for the shared object options and the
[Changelog](/guide/changelog/) guide for the versioning/commitlint pipeline.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/ci/changelog.md
---
# Changelog workflow

The `ci.changelog` workflow (`changelog.yml`) generates the changelog and applies
the version bump. It runs on every push to `ci.changelog.branches.dev` (or
`main` when `dev` is not set), then commits the updated `CHANGELOG.md` files and
`package.json` versions back to the branch.

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
toolchain: {
    ci: {
        changelog: {
            branches: { main: 'main', dev: 'dev' },
            pushBranches: ['dev'], // optional per-workflow override
        },
    },
}
```

`ci.changelog` is also the changelog **pipeline** config. Its options are
documented in the [Changelog](/guide/changelog/) guide:

* [Branches](/guide/changelog/branches)
* [commitlint](/guide/changelog/commitlint)
* [Versioning](/guide/changelog/versioning)
* [CLI](/guide/changelog/cli)

The workflow is opt-in (`ci.changelog: true` or an object). `ci.changelog:
false` leaves it unmanaged; `ci.changelog.commitlint: false` still generates the
workflow but skips commitlint, its config and the local hook.

`ci.changelog` inherits the manual `toolchain.changelog` pipeline options when
it does not set them itself (for example `ci.changelog: true` or an
object that only sets workflow options like `pushBranches`). Explicit
`ci.changelog` options win; `branches` only exists on `ci.changelog`.

The workflow itself can target another vendor with `{ provider, workflow }`
(GitLab/Azure); the versioning/commitlint pipeline still lives in
`toolchain.changelog` (or the `ci.changelog` object options), not in the vendor
workflow. See [Workflow settings](/guide/ci/settings#vendor-workflows).

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/ci/ci.md
---
# CI checks

The `ci.ci` workflow (`ci.yml`) is the repository's main check. It runs on
pushes to `ci.changelog.branches.main` and on pull requests to the generated
branch globs, and its default job:

1. checks out the repo, then sets up the toolchain: a Vite/Vite+ project uses
   [`voidzero-dev/setup-vp`](https://viteplus.dev/guide/ci) (which installs
   Vite+, Node.js and the package manager, then runs `vp install`), while any
   other project sets up Node and Corepack and installs dependencies;
2. runs commitlint over the pushed range — **removed when commitlint is
   disabled** with `ci.changelog.commitlint: false`;
3. runs `dbx sync --check` so generated files cannot drift;
4. runs the package manager's `build`.

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
toolchain: {
    ci: {
        ci: {
            pullRequestBranches: ['main', 'dev', 'release/**', 'dependabot/**'],
            steps: {
                after: [
                    { name: 'Format + lint', run: 'yarn check:fix' },
                    { name: 'Test', run: 'yarn test' },
                ],
            },
        },
    },
}
```

Use [Workflow settings](/guide/ci/settings) for the shared options, including
how a project is detected as Vite+ and how to force or disable that setup. The
workflow is opt-in: `ci: { ci: true }` writes it; omitting `ci.ci` (or setting it
to `false`) leaves the file unmanaged. Set `provider` (`gitlab`/`azure`) with a
complete `workflow` object to write that vendor's pipeline instead.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/ci/dependabot.md
---
# Dependabot

`ci.dependabot` writes `.github/dependabot.yml` so GitHub keeps the project's
dependencies and pinned actions up to date, and can additionally enable native
Dependabot security updates with grouped or individual PRs. Like every workflow
it is **opt-in**: omit it (or set it to `false`) and the file is left unmanaged.

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
toolchain: {
    ci: {
        dependabot: true,
    },
}
```

By default the config watches the **GitHub Actions** and **npm** ecosystems at
the repository root with a **weekly** schedule. The `github-actions` entry also
keeps pinned actions such as
[`voidzero-dev/setup-vp`](https://viteplus.dev/guide/ci#automatic-version-updates),
`actions/checkout` and `actions/setup-node` current, so a Vite+ CI setup does not
drift.

```yaml [.github/dependabot.yml]
version: 2
updates:
    - package-ecosystem: github-actions
      directory: /
      schedule:
          interval: weekly
    - package-ecosystem: npm
      directory: /
      schedule:
          interval: weekly
```

## Security updates

GitHub's native Dependabot security updates open PRs for vulnerable
dependencies. They are a **repository setting**, not a `dependabot.yml` option,
so `ci.dependabot.security` does two things:

1. Adds a `security-updates` group (`applies-to: security-updates`) to the
   generated `dependabot.yml` when the PR strategy is `grouped`.
2. Generates `.github/workflows/dependabot-security.yml`, which runs on the
   Dependabot schedule and enables (or disables) Dependabot security updates
   through the REST API. When a severity threshold is configured, it also
   dismisses alerts below that threshold so Dependabot does not open PRs for
   them.

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
toolchain: {
    ci: {
        dependabot: {
            security: {
                vulnerabilities: { severity: 'high' },
                pr: { strategy: 'grouped' },
            },
        },
    },
}
```

`security: true` is shorthand for:

```ts
security: {
    vulnerabilities: { severity: 'all' },
    pr: { strategy: 'grouped' },
    workflow: true,
}
```

With the grouped strategy the generated config contains:

```yaml [.github/dependabot.yml]
groups:
    security-updates:
        applies-to: security-updates
        patterns:
            - '*'
```

Choosing `pr: { strategy: 'individual' }` omits that group, so Dependabot opens
one security PR per update. User-defined groups with
`applies-to: security-updates` are kept as-is.

The workflow needs a **repository administrator** token to change the repository
setting. Create a `DBX_GITHUB_TOKEN` secret with `administration: write`
(fine-grained) or the `repo` scope (classic). The workflow falls back to
`GITHUB_TOKEN` for the alert-dismissal step (which works with the workflow's
`security-events: write` permission), but `GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot enable the
repository setting. If the token is missing, the step logs a warning and leaves
the setting untouched.

`severity` is applied by the generated workflow because `dependabot.yml` has no
severity filter. It dismisses lower-severity alerts with the `not_used` reason;
if you later lower the threshold, re-open those alerts manually. For native
pre-alert filtering, use GitHub's auto-triage rules and set
`security: { workflow: false }` so the toolchain does not manage the repository
setting.

Set `security: { vulnerabilities: false }` to disable Dependabot security
updates; the generated workflow calls the disable endpoint. Set
`security: { workflow: false }` to leave both the repository setting and alert
dismissal to you.

> `allow` also filters security updates. If you use it to narrow version
> updates, include `'*'` (or every package you want protected) so vulnerability
> PRs are not restricted. `update-types` rules still only affect version
> updates, so the usual major-version `ignore` does not suppress security fixes.

## Options

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
toolchain: {
    ci: {
        dependabot: {
            schedule: 'daily',
            directories: ['/', '/packages/api'],
            ecosystems: ['github-actions', 'npm'],
            labels: ['dependencies'],
            openPullRequestsLimit: 5,
            groups: {
                minor: { 'update-types': ['minor', 'patch'] },
            },
            security: {
                vulnerabilities: { severity: 'high' },
                pr: { strategy: 'grouped' },
            },
            // Allow only the packages you actually want updated...
            allow: {
                npm: [
                    { 'dependency-name': 'vite' },
                    { 'dependency-name': 'vite-plus' },
                ],
                'github-actions': [{ 'dependency-name': '*' }],
            },
            // ...and never cross a major version automatically.
            ignore: {
                npm: [
                    {
                        'dependency-name': '*',
                        'update-types': ['version-update:semver-major'],
                    },
                ],
            },
            dir: '.github', // default
            filename: 'dependabot.yml', // default
        },
    },
}
```

| Option                              | Default                     | What it does                                               |
| ----------------------------------- | --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `schedule`                          | `weekly`                    | `daily`, `weekly` or `monthly`.                            |
| `directories`                       | `['/']`                     | Directories to scan.                                       |
| `ecosystems`                        | `['github-actions', 'npm']` | Package ecosystems.                                        |
| `labels`                            | none                        | Labels added to the update PRs.                            |
| `openPullRequestsLimit`             | Dependabot default (5)      | Maximum open update PRs per entry.                         |
| `groups`                            | none                        | Update groups (patterns / update types).                   |
| `security`                          | off                         | Enable security updates (boolean or object).               |
| `security.vulnerabilities`          | `true`                      | Open PRs for vulnerable dependencies.                      |
| `security.vulnerabilities.severity` | `all`                       | Keep alerts at/above a severity, or the listed severities. |
| `security.pr.strategy`              | `grouped`                   | `grouped` (one PR per ecosystem) or `individual`.          |
| `security.workflow`                 | `true`                      | Generate the workflow that applies the setting.            |
| `allow`                             | none                        | Allow rules (an array, or keyed by ecosystem).             |
| `ignore`                            | none                        | Ignore rules (an array, or keyed by ecosystem).            |
| `dir` / `filename`                  | `.github/dependabot.yml`    | Generated path overrides.                                  |
| `enabled`                           | `true` when present         | Set `false` to opt out explicitly.                         |

A hand-written `.github/dependabot.yml` without the generated header is left
untouched and reported as a conflict, exactly like a hand-written workflow.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/ci/issues.md
---
# Issues

The `ci.issues` workflow (`issues.yml`) normalizes new issue titles from the
issue's labels: a bug-labelled issue gets a `[bug]` prefix, an
enhancement/feature/feat-labelled issue gets `[feat]`; issues without either
label are left untouched.

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
toolchain: {
    ci: {
        issues: true,
    },
}
```

The workflow is opt-in and only runs on `issues: opened`. It needs the
`issues: write` permission, which the generated default declares.

Use [Workflow settings](/guide/ci/settings) to change its triggers or add jobs,
or set `provider` with a complete GitLab/Azure `workflow` to target another
vendor.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/ci/releases.md
---
# Releases

The generated `ci.release` workflow (`release.yml`) opens a release PR whose body
is the **aggregated changelog**: every entry from the last released version up to
the latest one, not just the newest entry. So a release that skips versions
(eg. `v1.7.0` → `v1.7.8`) still documents `1.7.1`–`1.7.8` in one place.

The body is produced by `dbx changelog --release-body <version>`, which only
considers versions that actually appear in `CHANGELOG.md` (so unrelated
CI/calendar tags are ignored). For a first release, when there is no prior
version, it falls back to the newest changelog entry instead of the whole file.

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
toolchain: {
    ci: {
        release: { pushBranches: ['main'] },
    },
}
```

The workflow is opt-in. Use [Workflow settings](/guide/ci/settings) to override
the job's extra steps/jobs or supply a fully hand-authored workflow. It can also
be a complete GitLab/Azure pipeline via `{ provider, workflow }`.

## Grouped release bodies

By default each release body stops at the previous released version. When a
project publishes prereleases (for example `3.0.0-beta.1` … `3.0.0-beta.16`
before `3.0.0`), the stable GitHub Release would only mention the changes since
the last beta. Set `release.group` to treat every version since the previous
**published** release as one version:

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
toolchain: {
    ci: {
        changelog: {
            versioning: { target: 'individual', prerelease: 'beta' },
            release: { group: true },
        },
    },
}
```

* A **stable** release skips prerelease versions when it picks the boundary, so
  all betas since the last stable release are merged into one body. Version
  headings and duplicate section groups are never repeated; the newest
  `### Package changes` footer wins because it already covers the whole range.
* A **prerelease** release still stops at the previous prerelease, so each beta
  lists only its own changes instead of repeating the whole cycle.
* A **first release** (no published release yet) groups every changelog entry
  when grouping is enabled; without grouping it keeps the newest-entry
  fallback.
* Missing tags are tolerated: if no released version can be found, grouping
  selects the entries above the newest match, or the whole changelog when none
  matches.

When `gh` is available and the repository has published releases, the boundary
comes from them (drafts are excluded); otherwise it falls back to the local tags
merged into `HEAD`. The command is read-only, so re-running it produces the same
body.

### Overrides

| Setting                      | Effect                                                                                    |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `release.group`              | Enable grouped release bodies. **Default `false`.**                                       |
| `release.includePrereleases` | Let a prerelease bound a stable release's body (only the changes since that beta).        |
| `release.since`              | Explicit lower boundary version/tag (eg. `v1.2.0`); a missing version falls back to auto. |

The same options are available as one-off CLI flags:

```sh
dbx changelog --release-body 3.0.0 --release-group
dbx changelog --release-body 3.0.0 --release-since v3.0.0-beta.1
dbx changelog --release-body 3.0.0 --no-release-group
```

`--release-group` wins over the config for that run, and `--no-release-group`
turns a configured grouping off (useful for debugging).

With `versioning.target: 'individual'`, the root `CHANGELOG.md` remains the
aggregate release body: it lists every pushed commit, while package changelogs
stay scoped to their own package and are not merged into the GitHub Release.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/ci/settings.md
---
# Workflow settings

A workflow can be a boolean, a raw YAML string, a complete vendor workflow
(`{ provider, workflow }`), or a `WorkflowOptions` object. The object is merged
over the generated GitHub default, so you only describe what changes. These
options apply to every GitHub workflow (`ci`, `changelog`, `release`, `issues`,
`sync`).

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
toolchain: {
    ci: {
        ci: {
            enabled: true,
            pushBranches: ['main', 'next'],
            pullRequestBranches: ['main', 'release/**'],
            triggers: { schedule: [{ cron: '0 6 * * *' }] },
            tokens: { nodeVersion: '24' },
            extra: { permissions: { contents: 'read' } },
            steps: {
                after: [{ name: 'Lint', run: 'yarn lint' }],
            },
            jobs: {
                smoke: {
                    'runs-on': 'ubuntu-latest',
                    steps: [{ run: 'echo ok' }],
                },
            },
        },
    },
}
```

| Option                | What it does                                                                    |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `enabled`             | Enable/disable this workflow (default: enabled when present).                   |
| `provider`            | Vendor for a complete `workflow` object (default `github`).                     |
| `pushBranches`        | Replace `on.push.branches`.                                                     |
| `pullRequestBranches` | Replace `on.pull_request.branches`.                                             |
| `triggers`            | Merge extra `on.*` triggers.                                                    |
| `extra`               | Merge extra top-level keys (`permissions`, `concurrency`, `env`, ...).          |
| `steps`               | Inject steps before/after a job's generated steps (one group or per-job).       |
| `jobs`                | Merge extra complete jobs.                                                      |
| `tokens`              | Override workflow tokens (`nodeVersion`, `packageManager`, `yarnVersion`, ...). |
| `filename`            | Override the generated file name (default `ci.yml`, `release.yml`, ...).        |
| `dir`                 | Override the output directory (default `.github/workflows`).                    |

## Steps

`steps` accepts one group or an array of groups. A group targets a job id
(default: the first/primary job) and can add steps before or after the generated
ones:

```ts
steps: [
    { job: 'ci', before: [{ name: 'Install extras', run: 'yarn add -D foo' }] },
    { job: 'ci', after: [{ name: 'Smoke', run: 'yarn smoke' }] },
];
```

## Tokens

The default workflow templates use {{ token }} replacements. `tokens` merges
over the project-wide values, so one workflow can use a different Node version or
package manager without changing `project`. Overriding `packageManager` switches
to that manager's default version unless you also set `packageManagerVersion`
(or the legacy `yarnVersion` alias).

## Vite+ projects

For a Vite/Vite+ project the generated workflows install `vp` with the
[`voidzero-dev/setup-vp`](https://viteplus.dev/guide/ci) integration instead of
the Node/Corepack/package-manager install steps. The GitHub Action also sets up
the project's Node.js version and the package manager, and runs `vp install`.

A project is detected as Vite/Vite+ when any of these is true:

* its `package.json` declares `vite-plus` (checked up to the repository root, so
  a hoisted workspace dependency counts);
* it has a `vite.config.*` at the project root;
* the toolchain's `vite` section is enabled (the dbx-managed Vite+ mode).

Override the detection per workflow with `tokens.vitePlus` (`true` forces the
setup-vp path, `false` keeps the Node/Corepack path). `tokens.setupVpVersion`
pins a different exact `setup-vp` release or commit SHA; the action has no moving
tag, so always pin an exact version.

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
toolchain: {
    ci: {
        ci: { tokens: { setupVpVersion: 'v1.30.0' } },
        sync: { tokens: { vitePlus: false } },
    },
}
```

The other vendors use their own `setup-vp` integration when `setup: true` is set
on a complete pipeline:

* **GitLab** adds the reusable remote template to `include` (`setup-ref` pinned
  to the same version) and adds `extends: .setup-vp` to every job. The template
  does not install Node.js, so the pipeline still gets a `node:<nodeVersion>`
  image.
* **Azure** adds the `setupVp` repository resource (`ref` pinned to the version)
  and the `azure/setup-vp.yml@setupVp` template step with
  `setupRef`/`nodeVersion`/`cache`/`runInstall`. A job that already defines a
  checkout or the template step is left alone.

```yaml [.gitlab-ci.yml]
include:
    - remote: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/voidzero-dev/setup-vp/v1.22.0/gitlab/setup-vp.yml
      inputs:
          setup-ref: v1.22.0
image: node:22
test:
    extends: .setup-vp
    stage: test
    script: [yarn test]
```

Set `tokens.vitePlus: false` on a vendor workflow to keep its Node/Corepack
setup instead.

## Raw YAML

A string is used as the workflow file's exact content. It is not merged, not
token-replaced and gets no generated header; an empty string disables it.

## Vendor workflows

Set `provider` (`github`, `gitlab` or `azure`) with a complete `workflow` object
to write another CI vendor's pipeline instead of the generated GitHub default.
The object is written as-is (with the toolchain's {{ token }} replacements
applied), so it must be a complete pipeline:

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
toolchain: {
    ci: {
        ci: {
            provider: 'gitlab',
            workflow: {
                stages: ['test'],
                test: { stage: 'test', script: ['yarn test'] },
            },
        },
        release: {
            provider: 'azure',
            workflow: {
                trigger: ['main'],
                pool: { vmImage: 'ubuntu-latest' },
                steps: [{ script: 'yarn build' }],
            },
        },
    },
}
```

The default paths are `.gitlab-ci.yml` and `azure-pipelines.yml` (GitHub keeps
`.github/workflows/<id>.yml`); `filename` and `dir` override them. A complete
vendor workflow defines its own triggers, so the `ci.changelog.branches` defaults
do not rewrite them. `dbx workflow` runs each workflow with its vendor CLI
(`glab ci run`, `az pipelines run --name <pipeline>`, or `gh workflow run`).

Set `setup: true` to inject the provider-specific setup before the pipeline's own
steps: GitHub gets the checkout/Node/Corepack/install steps, GitLab gets a
`node:<version>` image plus a `before_script`, and Azure gets `UseNode@1` plus an
install script. It defaults to `false`, so the workflow is written as-is.

If a hand-written `.gitlab-ci.yml` / `azure-pipelines.yml` already exists, sync
leaves it untouched and records a workflow conflict, exactly like a GitHub
workflow. Set `ci.<id>: { enabled: false }` to opt out explicitly.

## Custom workflows

Add any number of extra workflows with `toolchain.ci.custom`, keyed by workflow
id. A custom workflow is enabled by **presence** (there is no boolean form): a
string is written verbatim, a complete vendor workflow (`{ provider, workflow }`)
is written as-is, or an object is merged over an empty GitHub workflow — build it
with `triggers`, `extra` and `jobs` (plus `filename` / `dir`):

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
toolchain: {
    ci: {
        custom: {
            deploy: {
                triggers: { workflow_dispatch: {}, push: { branches: ['main'] } },
                filename: 'deploy.yml', // default: deploy.yml
                dir: '.github/workflows', // default
                jobs: {
                    deploy: {
                        'runs-on': 'ubuntu-latest',
                        steps: [
                            { uses: 'actions/checkout@v4' },
                            { run: 'yarn deploy' },
                        ],
                    },
                },
            },
        },
    },
}
```

This writes `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` and manages it like any built-in
workflow (the generated header is prepended, and `dbx sync --check` tracks it).
Set `setup: true` to inject the shared checkout/Node/Corepack/install steps into
each job; steps the job already defines are not duplicated.

## Existing workflows

If a generated workflow path already contains a hand-written workflow that dbx has
never managed (no manifest entry and no generated header), `dbx sync` leaves it
untouched, warns, and records the conflict in `.dbx/toolchain/manifest.json`.
Set `ci.<id>: { enabled: false }` (or, for a custom workflow,
`ci.custom.<id>: { enabled: false }`) to make the opt-out explicit. The file is
also never deleted when the workflow is later disabled, because dbx did not
create it. Use `dbx workflow --list` (or `--list --json`) to see the enabled
workflows and their exact paths; `dbx workflow <id|file>` honours `filename` and
`dir` overrides.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/ci/sync.md
---
# Sync

The `ci.sync` workflow (`sync.yml`) verifies that every generated file is up to
date: it runs `dbx sync --check` on pushes (to both the `main` and `dev` branch
globs) and on pull requests. A drift in a workflow, tsconfig, `vite.config.ts`
or any other managed file fails the job.

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
toolchain: {
    ci: {
        sync: true,
    },
}
```

The workflow is opt-in. The `ci` check workflow also runs `dbx sync --check`, so
`sync.yml` is useful when you want the check to run on pull requests without the
full build. See [Workflow settings](/guide/ci/settings) for trigger overrides, or
set `provider` with a complete GitLab/Azure `workflow` to target another vendor.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/migrations.md
---
# Migrations

`dbx migrate` converts a project's tooling config from another tool to
**Oxc** (Oxfmt + Oxlint), or folds an existing Oxc/Vite config into
`dbx.config.*`. Migrations are pluggable — adding a source tool is a
matter of implementing one interface.

```sh
dbx migrate:list                       # what's available + detected
dbx migrate --from biome               # dry-run
dbx migrate --from biome --write       # writes the oxc config
dbx migrate --from biome --target vite --write
dbx migrate --from biome --from prettier --write  # several sources
dbx migrate --from oxc --write         # fold .oxfmtrc/.oxlintrc into dbx.config
dbx migrate --from all                 # every detected source
dbx migrate --check                    # CI: exit 1 when the oxc config is stale
dbx migrate --from eslint --online --write   # flat config via @oxlint/migrate
```

`dbx migrate` is a dry-run unless you pass `--write` (or `--check`). `--from`
is repeatable; `--from all` (or omitting it) selects every detected source.

## Upgrading from v2

See the [v2 → v3 migration guide](/guide/migrations/v2-v3).

## Upgrading from v1

See the [v1 → v2 migration guide](/guide/migrations/v1-v2).

## Sources

| Source     | Notes                                                                                                                                                        |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `biome`    | Formatter options, `files.includes` negations → `ignorePatterns`, **`organizeImports.groups` → Oxfmt `sortImports`**, and a curated Biome → Oxlint rule map. |
| `prettier` | Prettier-compatible options transfer directly; Tailwind/PackageJson plugins detected; `.prettierignore` → `ignorePatterns`.                                  |
| `eslint`   | JSON configs map rule names + severities (`@typescript-eslint/*` → `typescript/*`); JS/flat configs use `@oxlint/migrate` with `--online --write`.           |
| `dprint`   | `dprint.json` layout + TypeScript options → Oxfmt.                                                                                                           |
| `oxc`      | Folds `.oxfmtrc.json` / `.oxlintrc.json` into `dbx.config.*`'s `toolchain.fmt.oxc` / `toolchain.lint.oxc`; `dbx sync` manages them again.                    |
| `vite`     | Folds a hand-written `vite.config.*` into `dbx.config.*`'s `toolchain.vite` (see below).                                                                     |

## Targets

* `--target files` (default) — writes `.oxfmtrc.json` and `.oxlintrc.json`.
* `--target vite` — folds the result into an existing `vite.config.ts`
  (inserting/replacing `fmt` and `lint`), which is what Vite+ reads.
* The `oxc` source targets `dbx.config.*` (`toolchain.fmt.oxc` /
  `toolchain.lint.oxc`, or `toolchain.vite.fmt/lint` when `--target vite`).

Unless `--target` is given, formatter/linter migrations route by what the
existing Vite config already owns:

* If `vite.config.*` (or an existing `toolchain.vite`) defines `fmt`/`lint`, the
  migrated options are merged into `toolchain.vite.fmt`/`toolchain.vite.lint`,
  and no top-level `toolchain.fmt`/`toolchain.lint` is created.
* Otherwise they are folded into the top-level `toolchain.fmt.oxc` /
  `toolchain.lint.oxc`, and `vite.fmt`/`vite.lint` are left undefined.

## Recursive migration

By default `dbx migrate` only touches the root (`--cwd`, or the current
directory). `--recursive` walks the discovered projects under the root and
migrates each one that has a **detected source**:

```sh
dbx migrate --from biome --from prettier --recursive --write
```

On an interactive terminal it first asks which projects to migrate with a
multi-select — every candidate is listed by its relative path (with its package
name as a hint), plus an **All projects** option. Non-interactive runs (piped
output, CI, or `--json`) migrate every candidate without prompting. A project is
a candidate when a migration matching `--from` (or any migration, for `all`/no
`--from`) is detected in its directory — so a workspace with its own
`biome.json` or `vite.config.*` is included, and one without is skipped.

## `vite.config`

The `vite` source moves a hand-written `vite.config.*` into `dbx.config.*`'s
`toolchain.vite`, so the whole Vite+ config lives in the one hand-authored config
and `dbx sync` writes a thin `vite.config.ts` shim that resolves it at load time:

```sh
dbx migrate --from vite          # dry-run: shows what would fold in
dbx migrate --from vite --write  # folds the object into toolchain.vite
dbx sync                         # writes the managed vite.config.ts shim
```

When the folded config already owns `fmt`, it adds `/vite.config.ts` to
`toolchain.vite.fmt.ignorePatterns`, so Oxfmt leaves the generated shim alone
(otherwise `vp fmt` would rewrite it and `dbx sync --check` would report drift).
When it does not, `vite.fmt` stays undefined; the default fmt ignores already
cover `**/vite.config.ts`.

It extracts the object literal passed to `defineConfig(...)` (or the
default-exported object) with a string-aware, balanced-paren scanner and
text-splices it into the nearest `dbx.config.*`: it inserts `vite: { ... }`, or
**deep-merges** into an existing `toolchain.vite` (nested objects are combined;
arrays and scalars from the vite config win), so its settings are kept. A
previous `config: false` opt-out is flipped to `config: true`, since the
hand-written file is being removed. When the config references imports, plugins
or any non-literal expression it is reported as **unmapped** and nothing is
written, rather than emitting broken output. A JSON `dbx.config.json` is also
left alone (the object is folded by hand).

When the project has a `vite.config.*` but **no** `dbx.config.*` (a workspace
that never had one), the migration creates a fresh `dbx.config.ts` holding the
folded `toolchain.vite`, wrapped in `defineConfig` from `@deltabox/toolchain`
(like the scaffold). A workspace resolves that import through the root's
installed dependency — in a self-hosted repo, via a root `portal:.` self-link.

The now-redundant `vite.config.*` is removed and recreated by `dbx sync` as a
shim that imports `defineConfig` from the project's own Vite package (`vite` or
`vite-plus`, detected from `package.json`). Pass `--ignore-vite-config-file` to
keep the original file.

### Nested configs

In a monorepo, pass `--recursive` to fold **each workspace's** own
`vite.config.*` into that workspace's `dbx.config.*` (creating one when it is
missing) instead of the root's:

```sh
dbx migrate --from vite --recursive --write
```

Without `--recursive`, only the root's `vite.config.*` is migrated and nested
ones are left alone. Detection is per project root (a directory with a
`package.json` or `dbx.config.*`, up to five levels deep), so a `vite.config.*`
in a deeper subdirectory of a project is not discovered. A workspace with no
`dbx.config.*` gets a fresh one holding just its `toolchain.vite`; it inherits
the rest of the config from the nearest ancestor at load time.

## Post-migration sync

A `--write` run finishes by regenerating the project's toolchain-managed files
(the same files `dbx sync` writes) for every project it changed — so a migrated
project is immediately consistent, eg. the managed `vite.config.ts` shim appears
right after folding a hand-written config. Two flags narrow that step:

| Flag                     | Effect                                                                    |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--ignore-managed-files` | Skip the post-migration sync entirely; managed files are left untouched.  |
| `--ignore-changelog`     | Run the sync but drop the `changelog` task (workflows, commitlint, hook). |

The sync only runs after `--write`; a dry-run reports what it would do instead.

## Package scripts

`dbx migrate` migrates the tooling **files**; the matching `package.json` scripts
are a small follow-up. The common swaps:

| Before                   | After                       |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------- |
| `biome format --write .` | `dbx fmt`                   |
| `biome check --fix .`    | `dbx lint --fix`            |
| `turbo build`            | `dbx run -r build`          |
| `turbo typecheck`        | `dbx run -r typecheck`      |
| `turbo test`             | `dbx run -r test`           |
| `turbo dev`              | `dbx run -r --parallel dev` |

Then drop `@biomejs/biome` + `turbo` (and `biome.json` + `turbo.json`) and add
`@deltabox/toolchain` + `vite-plus`. The full walkthrough — recommended scripts,
the dependency diff and per-workspace tasks — is on the
[Package scripts](/guide/scripts) page.

## CI check

`--check` runs the migrations without writing and exits non-zero when a target
file is missing or differs from what the migration would produce, so a pipeline
can require that a repo is fully on Oxc:

```sh
dbx migrate --check || echo "still on Biome/etc — run migrate --write"
```

The check resolves the **effective** `dbx.config.*` (including an inherited
ancestor config), so a workspace that inherits `fmt`/`lint` from the root is not
asked to keep an intermediate `.oxfmtrc.json` / `.oxlintrc.json`. A disabled
section (`fmt: false`) does not count as owning the config.

`--online` allows network access: the ESLint migration shells out to
`@oxlint/migrate` to evaluate JS/flat configs (it writes `.oxlintrc.json`, so it
runs only together with `--write`).

## Honest output

Anything that cannot be mapped faithfully is reported instead of dropped:

```
unmapped (7):
  - organizeImports !lucide*: negated group members are approximated
  - linter.rules.suspicious.noUnknownAtRules: no Oxlint equivalent
```

## Programmatic

```ts
import { listMigrations, detectMigrations, runMigration } from '@deltabox/toolchain/migrate';

const detected = detectMigrations(process.cwd());
const result = await runMigration('biome', { cwd: process.cwd(), target: 'vite', write: true });
console.log(result.unmapped);
```

## Notes

`oxfmt --migrate biome`-style tools cover formatter options only; the pieces the
upstream tools skip (Biome `organizeImports`, Biome linter rules, Dprint) are
handled here.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/migrations/v1-v2.md
---
# Migrating from v1 to v2

**v2** focuses on a smaller, schema-driven config-generator API. Most runtime
features keep working, but the programmatic config-generator surface is a
breaking change.

## Breaking changes

### `ConfigScopes` and `ConfigScopeDef` are gone

Pass a `ConfigSchema` directly. It accepts a Zod schema, an untyped `Schema`, an
array of schemas, or a record keyed by scope.

```ts
// v1
const engine = createConfigEngine({
    scopes: {
        server: { zodSchema: serverConfig },
        cli: { zodSchema: cliConfig },
    },
});

// v2
const engine = createConfigEngine({
    schema: { server: serverConfig, cli: cliConfig },
});
```

`ConfigSchemaType` is the untyped `Schema` plus the toolchain's `ConfigMeta`.

### Render functions are internal

Use the `generateConfig*` functions or the engine methods. They return generated
contents and only write when you pass an output directory/path.

```ts
// v1
renderConfigTypes(scopes, { outputDir });
renderScopeMarkdown(scopes, { outDir });

// v2
generateConfigTypes(schema, { outputDir });
generateConfigMarkdown(schema, { outputDir });
```

Set `outputDir: false` (or omit it) to generate without writing.

### Schema maps were removed

`CONFIG_SECTION_SCHEMAS`, `CONFIG_TYPE_SCHEMAS` and
`CONFIG_SECTION_DESCRIPTIONS` were removed. Use `configSchema` (the section
schemas) or `dbxConfigSchema`, and read descriptions from each schema's
`.describe()` / `.meta()`.

### Metadata is the source of truth

Generators read `ConfigMeta` from Zod `.meta()` or from untyped schema nodes.
`env`/`path` are deprecated in favour of `envName`/`envPath`; `cliFlag` and
`cliFlagShort` customize CLI flags. Types can use `typeName` / `id` to control
the generated interface name.

### Collection names

* `collectEnvVars` → `collectVars`
* `collectRequiredEnvVars` → `collectRequired`
* `EnvVarDef` → `ConfigDef`
* `EnvValueType` → `ConfigValueType`
* engine `requiredEnvVars` → `requiredVars`
* `writeMarkdown({ outDir })` → `writeMarkdown({ outputDir })`

## Behaviour changes

* `toolchain.fmt` / `toolchain.lint` shorthand (`true` or `{ vscode: ... }`)
  now infers a tool from installed packages, then VS Code user settings, then
  falls back to Oxc defaults. Existing user config files are folded through the
  migration mappings instead of being overwritten.
* Formatter/linter conflict warnings use `fmt.conflict` / `lint.conflict`.
  Missing tools warn with `fmt.no-tool` / `lint.no-tool`.
* `fmt.vscode` / `lint.vscode` only add `editor.defaultFormatter`, language
  blocks and `editor.codeActionsOnSave`; use `{ overrides, exclude }` to adjust
  them.
* A custom logger can be supplied through `toolchain.logger.logger`.
* Changelog versioning supports custom bump rules/callbacks, over-bump opt-in,
  provider selection and commit credit/format options.

## tsconfig changes

### Resolve paths/references programmatically or from the CLI

**v2** adds a extends-aware resolver. Use it instead of hand-rolling alias parsing:

```ts
import { resolveTsconfig } from '@deltabox/toolchain/tsconfig';

const { alias, paths, references } = resolveTsconfig({
    root: process.cwd(),
    tsconfig: 'tsconfig.json', // optional; defaults to <root>/tsconfig.json
});
```

```sh
dbx tsconfig --json                       # { alias, paths, references }
dbx tsconfig --alias                      # Vite/Vitest resolve.alias entries
dbx tsconfig --paths                      # resolved compilerOptions.paths
dbx tsconfig --references                 # resolved project references
dbx tsconfig --tsconfig tsconfig.build.json
dbx tsconfig --root packages/app --no-extends
```

The resolver follows `extends` per field: a child can define `paths` while
inheriting `references` (or the reverse). When a config has no `baseUrl`, its
relative paths resolve from the config file that declares them.

### Stop editing generated `tsconfig.json` files

`dbx` owns the generated `tsconfig.json`; move customizations to
`tsconfig.default.json` or `toolchain.tsconfig.overrides` and re-run sync:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        tsconfig: {
            overrides: {
                base: { compilerOptions: { target: 'ES2022' } },
                default: { compilerOptions: { strict: true } },
                build: { compilerOptions: { declaration: true } },
                root: { compilerOptions: { types: ['node'] } },
            },
        },
    },
});
```

```sh
dbx sync --recursive
dbx sync --recursive --check
```

Overrides are deep-merged into the user-owned files (`baseFile`, `rootFile`,
`defaultFile`, `buildFile`; custom names are honoured). The first time a file is
patched, its original content is snapshotted in `.dbx/toolchain/manifest.json`
under `snapshots` (a tree of **relative** paths mirroring the repo), and the
applied override under `tsconfigOverrides`. Deleting an override key reverts it:
the original value comes back when the snapshot defines the key, otherwise the
key is removed (a value edited after the override set it is kept). A missing
target is skipped with a `tsconfig.missing-file` warning instead of being created.

```sh
dbx tsconfig --restore           # remove every applied override now
dbx tsconfig --restore build     # only base | root | default | build
```

`dbx reset` restores the overrides before it removes the manifest. The patched
files are never part of the manifest's managed `files`, so neither a sync nor a
reset deletes them. See [tsconfig → `overrides`](/guide/tsconfig#overrides).

`tsconfig.baseFile` (default `tsconfig.base.json`) names the root base tsconfig
that `overrides.base` targets. Use `tsconfig.extends` to choose what scaffolded
`tsconfig.base/default/build.json` files extend (for example
`build: './tsconfig.json'` to reuse path aliases in builds, at the cost of
pulling workspace source into the build).

### Sync task API

Custom sync tasks can use these additions:

* `SyncTask.watch` / `SyncTask.keep` accept a function of the config
  (`config => string[]`), so globs can follow configured file names.
* A `ManagedFile` returned with `track: false` is written and drift-checked like
  any other, but stays user-owned: it is not recorded in the manifest, never
  pruned by a later sync and never removed by `dbx reset`.
* `resolveWatchGlobs(tasks, config, projectType?)` (core) resolves the active
  tasks' inputs; `dbx watch --list [--json]` prints them, and the VS Code
  extension watches them (custom tsconfig names included) unless
  `deltabox.toolchain.watch` is set explicitly. Its default is now `[]`.
* `SyncContext.manifest` holds task metadata persisted in the manifest between
  syncs (`snapshots`, `tsconfigOverrides`); `SyncContext.check` is true for
  `dbx sync --check`.

### Do not hand-add workspace aliases

Keep `paths`/`references` in `tsconfig.workspaces.json`; the generator expands
them into each workspace. For Vite/Vitest, prefer Vite's native
`resolve.tsconfigPaths: true`, or pass `resolveTsconfig().alias` to
`resolve.alias`. If you created a `vitest.aliases.ts` during the transition,
delete it and use one of those two options.

## Vite and task changes

* Runtime shims are still the default (`vite.shim: 'runtime'`). Static shims
  (`vite.shim: 'static'`) serialize the config and import only `defineConfig`,
  useful when loading the shim without a built package.
* `vite.shimImport` changes the `resolveVite` import specifier for runtime
  shims. Relative values are resolved from the repo root and rewritten per
  generated config.
* `typecheck:ci` was removed; `typecheck` already uses the source tsconfig. Use
  `yarn typecheck` in CI and delete any `typecheck:ci` scripts or Vite+ tasks.
* The emulate test suite can be cleaned with `yarn test:clean`.

## Recommended upgrade steps

1. Replace `scopes` with `schema` in `createConfigEngine`.
2. Replace `render*` imports with `generateConfig*`.
3. Remove imports of the deleted schema maps; use `configSchema` or individual
   schema exports.
4. Rename `env`/`path` metadata to `envName`/`envPath` when convenient (the old
   names still work).
5. Remove hand-written `tsconfig.json` aliases and move them to
   `tsconfig.workspaces.json`; run `dbx sync --recursive`.
6. Replace any custom tsconfig path parser with `resolveTsconfig()` (or
   `dbx tsconfig --json`).
7. Delete `vitest.aliases.ts` if present; enable
   `resolve.tsconfigPaths: true` or use `resolveTsconfig().alias`.
8. Replace `typecheck:ci` with `typecheck` in scripts/CI.
9. Optionally move options you want managed in `tsconfig.base.json` /
   `tsconfig.workspaces.json` / the workspace default and build tsconfigs into
   `toolchain.tsconfig.overrides`, and keep committing
   `.dbx/toolchain/manifest.json` (it now holds their snapshots).
10. Run `yarn dbx sync`, `yarn config:types`, `yarn typecheck`, `yarn test` and
    `yarn dbx sync --recursive --check` after upgrading.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/migrations/v2-v3.md
---
# Migrating from v2 to v3

**v3** is a correctness and cleanup release.

Release notes
[here](https://github.com/deltabox-studio/toolchain/releases).
Full changelog
[here](https://github.com/deltabox-studio/toolchain/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).

## Table of contents

* [Migrating from v2 to v3](#migrating-from-v2-to-v3)
  * [The most important breaking changes](#the-most-important-breaking-changes)
  * [Some of the smaller changes](#some-of-the-smaller-changes)
  * [Breaking changes](#breaking-changes)
  * [New features](#new-features)
  * [Behaviour changes](#behaviour-changes)
  * [Recommended upgrade steps ](#recommended-upgrade-steps)

## The most important breaking changes

* The `tsdown` workspace rename to `pack`.
* The redesigned config-generator programmatic API.
* The config CLI program runtime replacing the commander-based CLI assembly.
* The `dbx()` Vite plugin becoming the preferred config path (available from the `@deltabox/toolchain/vite` subpath as usual).
* Vite+ (`vite-plus`) replacing the separate `vite`, `vitest` and `tsdown` dev
  dependencies (it bundles those tools behind `vp`).
* `@deltabox/toolchain` packages releasing independently instead of in lockstep.
* Vite+ projects configuring `pack`, `test` and `run.tasks` in `vite.config.*`
  instead of `tsdown.config.*`, `vitest.config.*` and `turbo.json`.
* `fmt`/`lint` moving into `vite.config.*` in Vite+ mode.

## Some of the smaller changes

* Improved changelog and release notes formatting.
* Managed `tsconfig.json` now declaring `include`/`exclude`/`compilerOptions.types` from extended tsconfig.
* UTF-8 BOM support (great for Windows Powershell users).
* Dockerfiles that build from a fresh scaffold.
* Scaffold-only Docker generation.
* `--online` for online templates.
* Stricter nested/configless inheritance and VS Code discovery.
* The `dbx.config.*` format itself is unchanged, so most projects only need to update the dependency and re-run `dbx sync`.
* Idempotent CI releases.

## Breaking changes

### The `tsdown` workspace is now `pack`

The workspace package `@deltabox/toolchain-tsdown` is renamed to
`@deltabox/toolchain-pack`, and the umbrella subpath
`@deltabox/toolchain/tsdown` becomes `@deltabox/toolchain/pack`. The workspace
directory moves from `packages/tsdown` to `packages/pack` and the commitlint
scope changes from `tsdown` to `pack`.

The underlying bundler is still tsdown, so `baseTsdownConfig` and
`createPostBanner` keep their shape. Replace the import specifier:

```diff [tsdown.config.ts]
-import { baseTsdownConfig } from '@deltabox/toolchain/tsdown';
+import { baseTsdownConfig } from '@deltabox/toolchain/pack';
```

and the workspace dependency for maintainers/contributors:

```diff [package.json]
-"@deltabox/toolchain-tsdown": "workspace:*",
+"@deltabox/toolchain-pack": "workspace:*",
```

`createTsdownConfig` now takes one options object instead of an
`(overrides, banner)` pair:

```diff [tsdown.config.ts]
-const config = createTsdownConfig({ format: ['cjs'] }, { name: 'Myapp' });
+const config = createTsdownConfig({
+    overrides: { format: ['cjs'] },
+    banner: { name: 'Myapp' },
+});
```

### Vite+ projects: `pack`, `test` and `run.tasks` live in `vite.config.*`

**This only applies when the project uses Vite+** (`vite-plus` and Vite+'s
`vite.config.*`). If the project is not on Vite+, keep the standalone
`tsdown.config.*`, `vitest.config.*` and `turbo.json` files as they are.

In a Vite+ project, the bundler, test runner and task runner read their
configuration from `vite.config.*`. Move each standalone config into the
matching Vite+ block, then delete the old file:

```diff [tsdown.config.ts → vite.config.ts]
# tsdown.config.ts
-import { defineConfig } from 'tsdown';
-
-export default defineConfig({
-    entry: ['src/index.ts'],
-    dts: true,
-    format: ['esm', 'cjs'],
-});

# vite.config.ts
+import { defineConfig } from 'vite-plus';
+
+export default defineConfig({
+    pack: {
+        entry: ['src/index.ts'],
+        dts: true,
+        format: ['esm', 'cjs'],
+    },
+});
```

```diff [vitest.config.ts → vite.config.ts]
# vitest.config.ts
-import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
-
-export default defineConfig({
-    test: {
-        include: ['src/**/*.test.ts'],
-        environment: 'node',
-    },
-});

# vite.config.ts
+import { defineConfig } from 'vite-plus';
+
+export default defineConfig({
+    test: {
+        include: ['src/**/*.test.ts'],
+        environment: 'node',
+    },
+});
```

```diff [turbo.json → vite.config.ts]
# turbo.json
-{
-    "tasks": {
-        "build": {
-            "dependsOn": ["^build"],
-            "outputs": ["dist/**"]
-        }
-    }
-}

# vite.config.ts
+import { defineConfig } from 'vite-plus';
+
+export default defineConfig({
+    run: {
+        tasks: {
+            build: {
+                command: 'vp build',
+                cache: { output: ['dist/**'] },
+            },
+        },
+    },
+});
```

Vite Task derives cross-package order from `package.json` dependencies, so
turbo's `^build` is not needed. A task name cannot also be a `package.json`
script: move the script into the task (or keep the script and skip the task
definition) so the name is declared once.

In a `dbx()` plugin project, add `pack` / `test` / `run.tasks` to the existing
`defineConfig` next to the `plugins` field; do not replace the plugin config. In config
mode, put the same keys under `toolchain.vite` in `dbx.config.*` and let
`dbx sync` write the Vite shim.

### The `dbx()` Vite plugin is the default config path

New scaffolds are configured through the `dbx()` Vite plugin. Import it from the
`@deltabox/toolchain/vite` subpath: `vite-plugin-dbx` is not published yet, so
the standalone package name is not available to install.

```diff
# invalid
-import { dbx, DBX_TASKS } from '@deltabox/toolchain-vite';
# correct
+import { dbx, DBX_TASKS } from '@deltabox/toolchain/vite';
```

The v2 `@deltabox/toolchain-vite` workspace is now `vite-plugin-dbx`, and the
umbrella subpath `@deltabox/toolchain/vite` re-exports it. A managed
`vite.config.*` shim is only written when the project declares its own `vite`
section.

In plugin mode the whole toolchain config lives in `vite.config.*`; there is no
`dbx.config.*` to author:

```diff [vite.config.ts]
+import { defineConfig } from 'vite-plus';
+
+import { dbx } from '@deltabox/toolchain/vite';
+
+export default defineConfig({
+    plugins: [
+        dbx({
+            toolchain: {
+                project: { name: 'app' },
+                fmt: true,
+                lint: true,
+            },
+        }),
+    ],
+});
```

`dbx.config.*` remains fully supported as the non-Vite fallback, so an existing
`dbx.config.*` project does not need to move. If you generate projects
programmatically, expect the generated `vite.config.*` to carry the plugin
instead of a separate `dbx.config.*`.

### Vite+ is the single dev dependency

**v3** no longer installs `vite`, `vitest` or `tsdown` for you. `vite-plus` is the
single dev dependency and provides `vp` (Vite, Vitest, Oxfmt, Oxlint, Rolldown
and tsdown); it is not bundled into `@deltabox/toolchain` at runtime. Replace the
individual dev dependencies with `vite-plus` and use `vp` / `vp run` for those
commands (declare it in the monorepo root, not in every single workspace):

```diff [package.json]
 {
     "devDependencies": {
-        "tsdown": "catalog:",
-        "vite": "catalog:",
-        "vitest": "catalog:"
+        "vite-plus": "catalog:"
     },
     "scripts": {
-        "build": "tsdown",
-        "test": "vitest run",
-        "lint": "oxlint .",
-        "format": "oxfmt ."
+        "build": "vp build",
+        "test": "vp test",
+        "lint": "vp lint",
+        "fmt": "vp fmt"
     }
 }
```

Workspace packages are released **individually** now: each public `packages/*`
workspace has its own version and `CHANGELOG.md`, and the release workflow
publishes any package whose version is not on npm yet. A consumer that depends on
a published subpackage should track that package's version instead of the
umbrella's.

### Git hooks use the Vite+ dispatcher

When `ci.changelog` is enabled, `dbx sync` writes the `commit-msg` hook to
`.vite-hooks/commit-msg` on a Vite+ project (it used to be `.husky/commit-msg`);
projects without Vite+ keep the husky fallback. To migrate:

```sh
yarn remove husky
rm -rf .husky
git config --unset core.hooksPath   # only if it still points at .husky/_
```

Replace `"postinstall": "husky"` with `"postinstall": "vp hooks enable"`, then
run `vp hooks enable` to install the `.vite-hooks/_` dispatcher. Add
`.vite-hooks/* text eol=lf` to `.gitattributes` on Windows. Staged checks move
to Vite+ too: add `.vite-hooks/pre-commit` running `vp staged` and a `staged`
block in the root `vite.config.ts` (`staged: { '*': 'vp check --fix' }`).

### Config generator programmatic API

The engine keeps the v2 `createConfigEngine({ schema })` shape, but v3 reshapes
the surrounding API:

* The ambient env declarations are now `dbx-env.d.ts` (previously `env.d.ts`).
  Update the `include`/`files` entries in your tsconfigs if you referenced the
  old file name.
* Runtime loading uses `parseConfig`, `parseEnvConfig` and `parseCliConfig`, plus
  `collect` and `loadConfig` / `loadConfigAsync` for file-backed configs. The
  source-specific `loadEnvConfig*`, `loadCliConfig*` and `loadFileConfig*` family
  (with `Sync`/`Async` variants) selects the file+env, file+CLI or file-only
  source set explicitly. The old
  `parseEnvTree` + `envString`/`envInt`/`envBool` accessors and `applyOverrides`
  remain available, but are legacy; prefer the parsers so env, CLI and overrides
  are validated through the schema.
* The engine groups its generators: `engine.env` (and `engine.env.types`),
  `engine.types`, `engine.markdown` (`.cli`, `.env`, `.file`), `engine.cli`
  (`.generate`, `.options`, `.program`), `engine.jsonSchema` and
  `engine.configJson`. `configCommands({ engine })` now also exposes `config:all`,
  and the standalone `generateConfig*` functions return content unless you pass an
  output path.
* The high-level CLI program is now part of the public API:
  `engine.cli.program.create()` returns a runnable `ConfigProgram` (with
  `createCommand()` for one command), and `createConfigProgram(commands,
  options?)` builds one from framework-agnostic `CliCommand[]`. `commander` is
  no longer used or exported. The standalone
  `generateConfigProgram(schema, options)` returns the generated command
  descriptors without building a program.
* JSON Schema generation can preserve Zod's `$ref`/`$defs` graph
  (`preserveDefs: true`), and the markdown/CLI generators expose more
  frontmatter, scope and reference options. Static schema defaults are also new.

The `engine.*` generator methods are grouped now:

```diff [scripts/generate-config-reference.ts]
-engine.writeConfigTypes({ outputDir: 'types' });
+engine.types.write({ outputDir: 'types' });

-engine.writeEnvTypes({ outputDir: 'types' });
+engine.env.types.write({ outputDir: 'types' });

-engine.writeMarkdown({ outputDir: 'docs/reference/configuration' });
+engine.markdown.write({ outputDir: 'docs/reference/configuration' });

-await engine.writeJsonSchema({ output: 'config.schema.json' });
+await engine.jsonSchema.write({ output: 'config.schema.json' });

-engine.buildConfigJson();
+engine.configJson.build();
```

The runtime side moves from the `parseEnvTree` + `env*` accessors to the schema
parsers:

```diff [src/config.ts]
-import { envInt, envString, parseEnvTree } from '@deltabox/toolchain/config';
+import { loadConfigAsync } from '@deltabox/toolchain/config';

-const tree = parseEnvTree(process.env, 'MYAPP_');
-const serverConfig = {
-    host: envString(tree, 'host', '0.0.0.0'),
-    port: envInt(tree, 'port', 3000),
-};
+const config = await loadConfigAsync({
+    cwd: process.cwd(),
+    parser: serverConfigSchema,
+    source: 'env',
+    envPrefix: 'MYAPP_',
+});
```

And the ambient env declarations change file name:

```diff [tsconfig.json]
 {
     "include": [
         "src",
-        "types/env.d.ts"
+        "types/dbx-env.d.ts"
     ]
 }
```

If you only consume the generated files, re-run the generators; if you imported
the engine, update the calls to the grouped API and the runtime parsers.

### CLI command descriptors and program runtime

v3 replaces the commander-based CLI assembly with the config program runtime.
Custom CLIs now build the same program the `dbx` binary uses:

```ts
import { configCommands } from '@deltabox/toolchain/config';

const program = engine.cli.program.create(() => configCommands({ engine }), {
    name: 'myapp',
    version: '1.0.0',
    globalOptions: [{ flags: '--json', description: 'Print JSON.' }],
    disableColors: ({ color }) => color === false,
});
await program.invokeAsync(process.argv.slice(2));
```

* Rename `ToolchainCommand` / `ToolchainOption(s)` annotations to
  `CliCommand` / `CliOption(s)`. Wrap inline descriptors in
  `defineCliCommand()` from `@deltabox/toolchain/shared`; this preserves the
  literal `options` tuple so `run` values are inferred. The
  `CliOptionValues<typeof options>` type exposes the same shape directly.
* `engine.cli.program.create()` builds schema-derived commands with typed
  `run({ config, values, context })`; `createCommand(scope, spec)` builds one
  config-backed command and `createCommand('name', spec)` builds a runtime-only
  one. The callback may be async. `engine.cli.generate()` / `.options()` remain
  the low-level option generators.
* If you used the v3 beta program names, `engine.cli.program.generate()` is now
  `create()` and the old `engine.cli.program.command()` builder is now
  `createCommand()`. The chain's `.command()` method for subcommands is
  unchanged.
* A built program exposes `invoke()` / `invokeAsync()`, `argv()`,
  `withContext()`, `globalOption()` / `globalOptions()`, `hook()` / `hooks()`,
  `bin`, `formatHelp()`, `formatError()` and `configure()`. `invoke()` throws
  when a handler, hook or `disableColors` resolver is async; use
  `invokeAsync()`.
* `configCommands()` remains library-only; `dbx` does not register a `config:*`
  group because each command needs a consumer-bound `ConfigEngine`.
* A command's `bin` field executes a relative/absolute binary instead of the
  in-process handler; `argv` overrides the invocation arguments for
  `program.invoke()`.

### Oxc configs live in `vite.config.*` in Vite+ mode

In a Vite+ project, `dbx sync` no longer writes standalone `.oxfmtrc.json` /
`.oxlintrc.json` files. The formatter and linter options live in the Vite config
(`toolchain.vite.fmt` / `toolchain.vite.lint`, or the root `fmt`/`lint`
sections), which Vite+ reads directly.

If an existing Vite+ project has standalone `.oxfmtrc.json` / `.oxlintrc.json`
files, fold them into the Vite config with `dbx migrate --from oxc --write`;
`dbx sync` will no longer write or prune them:

```diff [.oxfmtrc.json]
-{
-    "printWidth": 100,
-    "singleQuote": true
-}
```

```diff [.oxlintrc.json]
-{
-    "rules": {
-        "no-console": "warn"
-    }
-}
```

```diff [vite.config.ts]
 export default defineConfig({
     plugins: [
         dbx({
             toolchain: {
+                fmt: { oxc: { printWidth: 100, singleQuote: true } },
+                lint: { oxc: { rules: { 'no-console': 'warn' } } },
             },
         }),
     ],
 });
```

### Project templates are one module per template

The monolithic template module is gone. The supported programmatic surface from
`@deltabox/toolchain/project` (also re-exported by the umbrella) is:

```ts
import {
    createProjectTemplateFiles,
    isProjectTemplateId,
    PROJECT_TEMPLATE_IDS,
    type ProjectTemplateId,
} from '@deltabox/toolchain/project';
```

Look a template up through `PROJECT_TEMPLATE_IDS` / `createProjectTemplateFiles`
instead of importing a shared `qol` helper.

### Docker plans expose their copy sources

`resolveDockerPlan()` now returns `installSources` — the exact files the
Dockerfile copies before installing dependencies. Code that constructs a
`DockerPlan` by hand must provide it; prefer `resolveDockerPlan()` +
`dockerFiles()` instead:

```diff
-const plan: DockerPlan = buildPlan();
+const plan = resolveDockerPlan({
+    cwd: process.cwd(),
+    packageManager: 'yarn',
+});
```

```diff
 const plan: DockerPlan = {
     runtime: 'node',
-    // ...
+    installSources: ['package.json', 'yarn.lock', '.yarnrc.yml'],
+    // ...
 };
```

## New features

The v3 line also adds a large set of capabilities on top of v2, grouped by area:

### Config engine and CLI

* Schema-derived CLI programs through `engine.cli.program.create()`, with typed
  options, subcommands, inherited global options, help formatting and typed
  `run({ config, values, context })` handlers.
* Typed `CliCommand` descriptors (`defineCliCommand`) that infer option values
  from their flags, plus scoped CLI generation from config schemas.
* Source-specific config loaders (file, env and CLI argv) with base-value merging,
  so env/CLI values override file values without schema defaults replacing them.
  Multi-source selections and `envExpose` metadata are supported.
* Static schema defaults and generated `toolchain.hooks` from function schemas.
* `enabled` / `regenerate` controls on sections, the `loader` config section and
  `project.manageConfigless`.
* `dbx enable` / `dbx disable` and the `dbx enabled` command.
* A reusable CLI docs generator (`engine.markdown.cli`) for command references.
* `dbx test:repo`, plus readable spinners and surfaced Vite+ passthrough errors.

### Vite+, formatting and task running

* Vite+ (`vite-plus`) as the single dev dependency and `vp` / `vp run` as the
  task runner; the shared pack config and workspace aliases no longer need a
  separate `tsdown` dependency.
* `dbx fmt` / `dbx lint` route to the active formatter/linter, with better
  auto-detection of the configured tool.
* Oxfmt and Oxlint option types generated from the tools' vendored JSON schemas,
  and typed tool options plus changelog callbacks.
* Nested scaffolds leave `fmt` / `lint` to the root config instead of emitting
  their own blocks.
* Scaffolds opt into the catalog they write, so `dbx sync` keeps the catalog
  managed.

### Templates, scaffolding and Docker

* New quality-of-life builtin templates and project/template generators.
* Opt-in containerization for scaffolds (`--containerize`), including
  scaffold-only Docker generation.
* The new `@deltabox/toolchain-docker` package, wired into the umbrella; Docker
  plans now expose the exact `installSources` copied before installing.
* `--online` for online templates, with clearer opt-in behaviour.

### MCP

* An MCP server, installers for Claude, Codex, VS Code, OpenCode, Pi and custom
  directories, and the `dbx mcp:*` commands.

### Changelog and CI

* Opt-in Dependabot security updates and dependency-update workflows.
* `beforeVersion` / `afterVersion` lifecycle hooks.
* Changelog `intro` / `outro`, `minCommits`, nested `See more...` descriptions,
  release mode and collapsible bodies.
* Grouped release bodies (`changelog.release.group`) that roll every prerelease
  since the previous published release into one stable release entry.
* Scoped versioning options and configurable breaking-change detection.
* Batched GitHub metadata lookups (commit authors, PR credit, issue titles).
* Complete GitHub, GitLab and Azure workflow configs with autocomplete and
  dispatch through the vendor CLI.

### VS Code extension

* A scoped auto-sync mode, the action palette and the Actions view.
* Managed-file decorations and a reveal-active-project action.
* Plugin-mode projects, MCP install and improved sync UX; sync notifications,
  `sync all`, a migration target picker and `manageConfigless` support.
* A Docker prompt while scaffolding, plus generic format/lint actions and
  formatting settings.
* The workflow provider in the run picker.

## Behaviour changes

### Config inheritance is strictly opt-in

A nested `dbx.config.*` only inherits the sections it explicitly enables
(`fmt`, `lint`, `biome`, `changelog`, `catalogs`, `logger`); `project` metadata
is inherited except its identity fields.

Projects without their own `dbx.config.*` (or `dbx()` vite plugin in `vite.config.*`) are unmanaged by default;
pass `--configless` or set `project.manageConfigless: true`
to inherit the nearest ancestor config.

See [Nested configs](/guide/config/nested-configs).

```diff [packages/web/dbx.config.ts]
 export default defineConfig({
     toolchain: {
         project: { name: 'web' },
+        // v3: a nested config only inherits sections it opts into.
+        fmt: true,
+        lint: true,
     },
 });
```

```diff [dbx.config.ts]
 export default defineConfig({
     toolchain: {
         project: {
+            manageConfigless: true,
         },
     },
 });
```

### Online templates need `--online`

`dbx create --template <id>` and the `template:*` commands only resolve online
(npm/git/Vite+) sources when `--online` is passed.

Local and builtin templates work without it, and a local-only run never touches the network.

Scripts and CI that relied on implicit online resolution must add the flag:

```diff
-dbx create --template @org/template --name app
+dbx create --template @org/template --name app --online
```

### Toolchain enable/disable

A top-level `toolchain.enabled` switch is available. The boolean shorthand is
workspace-scoped:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
    plugins: [dbx({ toolchain: { enabled: false } })],
});
```

Config files and the inline `dbx()` plugin only accept the workspace scope; the
object form (`{ disabled, scope: 'global' | 'workspace' }`) is reserved for the
CLI/programmatic API and the VS Code extension.

`dbx enable`/`dbx disable` choose the workspace scope by default; pass `--global` to update
`~/.dbx/toolchain/cli/config.json`.

The project config takes precedence over both the CLI workspace setting and `.vscode/settings.json`.

### Dependabot security updates

`toolchain.ci.dependabot` now accepts an opt-in `security` setting. It adds the
security-update group to `.github/dependabot.yml` and generates
`.github/workflows/dependabot-security.yml` to enable GitHub's native security
updates and optionally dismiss alerts below a severity threshold.

```diff [dbx.config.ts]
 export default defineConfig({
     toolchain: {
         ci: {
             dependabot: {
+                security: {
+                    vulnerabilities: { severity: 'high' },
+                    pr: { strategy: 'grouped' },
+                },
             },
         },
     },
 });
```

`security: true` keeps every severity and groups PRs per ecosystem. The workflow
needs a `DBX_GITHUB_TOKEN` secret with repository admin access to change the
repository setting; `GITHUB_TOKEN` is used for alert dismissal.

Set `security: { workflow: false }` to manage the setting yourself, or
`security: { vulnerabilities: false }` to disable security updates. No migration
is required: without `security`, the generated `dependabot.yml` and behaviour
are unchanged.

### Managed-file regeneration

Every managed section now accepts `regenerate?: boolean` (default `true`). Set it
to `false` to skip that section in `dbx sync`: its files are neither written nor
drift-checked, and sync does not prune them.

User-owned files (`tsconfig.workspaces.json`, `tsconfig.build.json`)
are only seeded when missing; an existing file is never overwritten by the missing-file fallback.

```diff [dbx.config.ts]
 export default defineConfig({
     toolchain: {
-        tsconfig: true,
+        tsconfig: { regenerate: false },
     },
 });
```

### Changelog versioning

* `versioning.target: 'individual'` is idempotent. Commits already listed in a
  workspace's `CHANGELOG.md` are filtered out before deriving its bump, and a
  workspace with no new commits is skipped entirely. Re-running no longer bumps
  untouched workspaces or re-counts an old `feat` as a new minor.
* Workspace glob negation (`['packages/*', '!packages/private-*']`) is honoured.
* A UTF-8 BOM in any `package.json` (common with PowerShell/Notepad) no longer
  makes `dbx changelog` fail; the same BOM handling applies to local CLI
  discovery, providers, Prettier detection and the VS Code extension.
* The `### Package changes` footer now reads Yarn (`.yarnrc.yml`), pnpm
  (`pnpm-workspace.yaml`) and Bun (`package.json` `workspaces.catalog`) catalogs,
  including named catalogs.
* Running changelog from a nested workspace uses the repository root for the
  fallback commit/issue links instead of the workspace's own `package.json`.

If you version workspaces individually, opt excluded packages out of the glob:

```diff [dbx.config.ts]
 versioning: {
     target: 'individual',
-    workspaces: ['packages/*'],
+    workspaces: ['packages/*', '!packages/private-*'],
 },
```

### Docker

* Only files that exist when the Dockerfile is generated are copied:
  `package.json` plus the project's lockfile/workspace files. `.node-version*` is
  never assumed, and a missing lockfile is not copied.
* The declared package manager drives both the copy list and the install command.
  A Bun-runtime project with no declared manager installs with Bun; otherwise the
  declared manager wins (so `yarn.lock` is not paired with `bun install`). When a
  Bun-runtime project declares yarn/pnpm/npm, dependencies install in a
  `node:<version>` `deps` stage and the Bun image only builds.
* When there is no lockfile, the install runs without a frozen flag.

### Scaffolding and migrations

* `dbx project:init --out <dir>` (and `project:init:monorepo`) no longer inherits
  the current project's name when `--name` is omitted; it uses the target
  directory's basename. The in-place case still inherits `project.name`.
* `dbx migrate --check` resolves the effective (inherited) config, so a
  workspace inheriting `fmt`/`lint` from the root is not asked to keep an
  intermediate `.oxfmtrc.json` / `.oxlintrc.json`. A disabled section
  (`fmt: false`) does not count as owning the config.

### CLI and VS Code

* `--no-color` now also disables the configured help/error colours. A custom
  program can implement the same switch with the `disableColors` program option.
* `dbx sync --json` always emits a JSON envelope, including when the config
  failed to load (`{ results: [], upToDate: false, error }`).
* `dbx projects --max-depth` rejects non-numeric values instead of silently
  turning the limit into `NaN`; `--max-depth 0` still scans only the root.
* The VS Code extension walks up to the repository boundary for the project's
  `dbx`, checks every workspace root in a multi-root workspace, and keeps the
  project's CLI as the default (the bundled CLI is only the fallback).

### TypeScript declarations

* The shared tsdown base config externalizes declaration imports **as written**
  (`deps.dts.neverBundle: true`), so emitted `.d.ts` files reference bare
  package specifiers instead of build-machine absolute `node_modules` paths.
  Packages whose public types reference another package must declare it in
  `dependencies` (or `peerDependencies`).
* The base config also ships a Rolldown leak reporter. It scans emitted JS,
  declaration and textual asset chunks and fails the build by default when an
  absolute `node_modules` path appears. Configure it with the
  `nodeModulesLeakReporter` option (or `false` to disable it):
  `{ level: 'warn' | 'info' | 'silent', when: 'generateBundle' | 'writeBundle' | 'closeBundle' }`.
  `writeBundle` is the default; use `closeBundle` when a later plugin rewrites
  output in `writeBundle`. Non-fatal levels respect tsdown/rolldown's log level.
  The plugin is also exported as `createNodeModulesLeakReporter` for use in your
  own builds.

```diff [tsdown.config.ts]
 const config = createTsdownConfig({
     overrides: { format: ['cjs'] },
+    nodeModulesLeakReporter: { level: 'warn', when: 'writeBundle' },
 });
```

## Recommended upgrade steps

1. Update `@deltabox/toolchain` to v3 and replace the individual `vite`,
